No. The partially visible snapshot count is a visibility measurement. It does not report whether writers were globally paused or whether unaffected base-table partitions were rescanned. Those operational requirements would need their own supporting information; they are not established by running or describing this check.
Give me a concise statement of the activity that does not imply it has already succeeded.
“Stress-test the adopted CommitBarrier v1 with 100,000 concurrent retraction transactions and leader-transfer crashes, and count committed snapshots that expose retractions only partially.”
LeaderTransfer100K observed 7 partially visible snapshots across 100,000 transactions when failover reused unfenced prepare acknowledgments. How should I report that result?

Report the measured unit and the condition together: “LeaderTransfer100K observed 7 partially visible snapshots across 100,000 transactions when failover reused unfenced prepare acknowledgments.” Seven is a count of *snapshots*, not necessarily a count of affected transactions, retractions, or failovers. The finding identifies the acknowledgment reuse associated with those observations; it does not provide a more detailed failure trace.
What does a partially visible snapshot mean in this setting?

It means a committed snapshot exposed an incomplete combination of a transaction’s required retraction effects. Some effects were visible while other effects needed for the same committed view were not. Internal differences in when shards finish work do not count on their own; the issue is what a committed reader could observe.

LeaderTransfer100K reports 7 snapshots with partial visibility. It does not specify which particular base-table, outer-join, or aggregate effects differed in each snapshot.
Could I describe this as 7 partially visible retractions?

No. The reported count is 7 *partially visible snapshots*. One snapshot count does not tell us how many retraction transactions it involved, and the finding does not supply a separate count of partially visible retractions. Keeping the unit unchanged matters here.
What does the phrase “when failover reused unfenced prepare acknowledgments” add to the result?

It identifies the condition under which the 7 partially visible snapshots were observed. A prepare acknowledgment concerns whether shard work is ready to support a transaction’s later visibility; calling the reused acknowledgments “unfenced” indicates that their reuse was not excluded across the relevant failover boundary.

The result does not specify the acknowledgment records, the sequence of failovers, or exactly how any individual snapshot came to be partially visible. It is more precise to retain the stated condition than to invent those details.
Does this say that the prepare acknowledgments were never durable?

No. “Unfenced” and “not durable” are different claims. The observation says failover reused unfenced prepare acknowledgments. It does not say those acknowledgments were absent from durable storage or specify what durability guarantees they had. Durability alone would not answer whether an acknowledgment may be reused inappropriately across a failover boundary.
Does the result tell us how many leader-transfer crashes occurred?

No. It names a failover condition and gives the number of transactions, 100,000, and the number of partially visible snapshots, 7. It does not give a crash or failover count. The 7 should not be relabeled as 7 crashes.
Could one failover have been associated with more than one of the 7 snapshots?

The finding does not say how the 7 snapshots were distributed across failovers. More than one snapshot per failover is a possibility, but so are other distributions; none can be reported as an observed detail from this statement. The defensible claim is the aggregate count and its stated condition.
If a snapshot later became complete, would the earlier partial visibility still matter?

Yes. The observation concerns committed snapshots at the time they were visible. A later coherent snapshot would not change the fact that an earlier committed snapshot was partially visible. The reported 7 is therefore not a claim about the final view after all 100,000 transactions.
What can I conclude about atomic visibility from a nonzero snapshot count?

Atomic visibility did not hold for every committed snapshot observed in LeaderTransfer100K: 7 were partially visible under the stated failover condition. That conclusion is bounded to this observation. It does not identify every affected transaction or establish how other failure conditions behave.
Does this observation tell us that every outer join or aggregate was wrong?

No. It reports 7 partially visible snapshots, not the correctness of every view value across the run. Partial visibility can affect the snapshot consistency required for outer joins and aggregates, but the finding does not enumerate which results were affected or provide a full comparison of all results against recomputation.
Should I call the reuse of unfenced acknowledgments the sole root cause?

The supplied result identifies it as the condition when partial visibility was observed. It does not establish that no other factors contributed or give enough detail to describe a complete causal chain. Saying “when failover reused unfenced prepare acknowledgments” preserves what was reported without claiming a sole root cause.
How do I avoid implying that all 100,000 transactions were partially visible?

Keep the counts attached to their own units: 100,000 transactions were in LeaderTransfer100K, and 7 partially visible *snapshots* were observed. The result does not say that 7 transactions—or all 100,000 transactions—were partially visible.
Can you give me a concise version that preserves both the nonzero finding and its limit?

“LeaderTransfer100K observed 7 partially visible snapshots across 100,000 transactions when failover reused unfenced prepare acknowledgments; the result does not specify how many transactions or failovers those snapshots involved.”

My hypothesis is that epoch-fenced prepare acknowledgments and recovery-validated commit barriers should eliminate partial snapshots during 100,000 leader-transfer transactions. What, precisely, am I predicting?

You are predicting that the committed snapshots observed during those 100,000 leader-transfer transactions will contain no partial transaction effects. In the multi-shard retraction setting, a committed snapshot must not expose a retraction on one affected part of the view while withholding another required effect of that same transaction.

The proposed protections are epoch-fenced prepare acknowledgments and commit barriers validated during recovery. “Should eliminate” is a hypothesis, not a report that the run has occurred or that zero partial snapshots have been observed.
What does the epoch fence contribute to a prepare acknowledgment?

Conceptually, it makes the acknowledgment meaningful only within an appropriate leadership epoch. When leadership changes, an acknowledgment associated with an earlier epoch must not automatically be treated as proof that a newly recovering leader may expose the transaction. The fence is intended to prevent an acknowledgment from being accepted outside the circumstances in which it was valid.

The hypothesis does not specify how epochs are assigned, recorded, or compared. It names the protection needed, rather than a particular fencing protocol.
Does fencing mean that prepared work from an earlier epoch must always be thrown away?

No such requirement follows from the hypothesis. Fencing an acknowledgment concerns whether that acknowledgment may authorize progress across an epoch boundary. It does not, by itself, say that recoverable staged work must be discarded. A recovery process could need to examine that work while deciding what can safely be made visible.

The hypothesis leaves the treatment of earlier-epoch staged work unspecified; its prediction concerns the committed snapshots readers ultimately observe.
How is an epoch-fenced acknowledgment different from an acknowledgment that was merely replicated?

Replication concerns preserving the acknowledgment; fencing concerns whether it remains valid for the leadership context in which someone tries to use it. A replicated record can survive a transfer and still require a validity check before it contributes to a visibility decision.

The hypothesis proposes the epoch fence as part of that check. It does not specify what information the replicated record contains or how the check is performed.
What does “recovery-validated” add to a commit barrier?

It means recovery should not assume that a barrier is safe to expose merely because some barrier-related state survived. Before recovered committed visibility relies on it, the barrier has to be checked against the transaction state needed to honor it across the affected shards. Otherwise, the recovered view might announce a transaction as visible without being able to present all of its required effects.

That describes the intended safety condition. The hypothesis does not prescribe a validation algorithm or identify every record it would consult.
Would the validation occur only if the barrier had not yet become visible before leader transfer?

The phrase “recovery-validated commit barriers” does not restrict the concern to unpublished barriers. Recovery has to preserve the meaning of whatever visibility boundary committed readers encounter: work not yet visible must not appear in part, and work already included in a committed snapshot must not recover in part.

The hypothesis does not define separate procedures for those cases. It predicts the absence of partial snapshots during the stated leader-transfer workload.
Can you explain why both pieces matter to the prediction without asserting that they already work?

The acknowledgment fence addresses whether evidence of shard preparation may be used after a leadership-epoch change. Barrier validation addresses whether the transaction’s visibility boundary remains supported by the required effects during recovery. Those are related but distinct questions: valid preparation evidence does not itself make a transaction visible, and a barrier should not expose effects it cannot safely support.

The hypothesis is that using both protections will eliminate partial snapshots in the 100,000 leader-transfer transactions. Whether they actually do so remains to be observed.
Where do shard-local staged MVCC deltas fit into this reasoning?

They are the work whose committed visibility needs control. A shard may stage an MVCC delta before other affected shards have finished their work. That difference in internal progress is not itself a partial snapshot. The issue arises if a committed reader sees some of those transaction effects while the rest remain unavailable or invisible.

Fenced acknowledgments and recovery-validated barriers are proposed as safeguards for deciding when those staged effects can be exposed coherently, particularly across leader transfer.
Suppose a retraction changes an outer-join match count and an aggregate contribution. Are those covered by “partial snapshots”?

They can be. A committed snapshot would be partial if it reflected the retraction in one required place but not in the related outer-join or aggregate effect belonging to that same transaction. For instance, a match-count transition that changes whether a null-extended result exists must not be visible at a transaction state incompatible with its other required effects.

The hypothesis addresses the visibility of such effects together. It does not claim that the count or aggregate delta is calculated correctly in the first place; correct computation is a separate requirement.
Does the hypothesis require all affected shards to finish at the same time?

No. It requires the committed snapshots to avoid partial exposure, not the underlying work to be simultaneous. Affected shards may stage or recover their transaction effects at different times, provided readers do not see an incomplete transaction as a committed result. The proposed fencing and recovery validation concern the boundary between that internal progress and committed visibility.
If a leader changes after one affected shard acknowledges but before another does, what would the hypothesis predict about the visible view?

It predicts that the transaction would not become partly visible as a committed effect merely because one shard acknowledged. The epoch fence would need to keep acknowledgments from being used outside their valid context, and the recovery-validated barrier would need to withhold visibility until the transaction can be exposed coherently.

That is a conditional illustration of what the hypothesis aims to achieve; no particular leader-transfer trace or observed behavior is supplied.
Could a recovered leader accept an earlier acknowledgment if it can validate it?

The hypothesis does not specify whether an acknowledgment from an earlier epoch may ever be accepted after further validation. It says acknowledgments are epoch-fenced, so their use across leadership changes must respect an epoch-based validity boundary. Any permitted recovery behavior would still have to support a barrier that does not expose partial snapshots.

Stating a categorical rule to reject or accept all earlier acknowledgments would add a protocol decision that is not provided here.
What should I count to assess “eliminate partial snapshots”?

Count committed snapshots that expose an incomplete set of required effects for a transaction. The hypothesis predicts a count of zero during the 100,000 leader-transfer transactions. That is a snapshot count, not automatically a count of transactions, acknowledgment records, leader transfers, or crashes.

The wording does not specify how many transfers occur or how the transactions are scheduled, so those quantities should remain unstated.
Is checking only the final snapshot after transaction number 100,000 sufficient?

No. “Eliminate partial snapshots during 100,000 leader-transfer transactions” concerns snapshots visible during the workload. A final coherent view would not rule out an earlier committed snapshot that briefly exposed part of a retraction. The relevant check is what committed readers could observe throughout the run, including around recovery boundaries.
If the count is zero, would that prove the entire outer-join and aggregate view matches full recomputation?

No. Zero partial snapshots would support the visibility prediction within the executions observed. An atomically visible transaction could still have an incorrectly calculated outer-join result or aggregate value. Full-recomputation equivalence at every committed snapshot is a broader correctness requirement; this hypothesis specifically concerns partial visibility during leader-transfer transactions.
Would the hypothesis say anything about globally pausing writers or rescanning unaffected base-table partitions?

It does not report either behavior. Epoch fencing and recovery validation describe proposed safeguards for visibility across leader transfer. They do not, by themselves, demonstrate progress without a global writer pause or show how view maintenance avoids scanning unaffected base-table partitions. Those remain distinct design constraints.
How strongly can I phrase the expected outcome right now?

Use predictive language: “Epoch-fenced prepare acknowledgments and recovery-validated commit barriers should eliminate partial snapshots during 100,000 leader-transfer transactions.” Avoid saying they *have eliminated* partial snapshots or that zero has already been measured. The hypothesis identifies a mechanism and a predicted outcome; it does not supply a completed test result.

Here is the recovery plan: fence stale prepare acknowledgments by epoch; recover transactions from replicated decisions, verifying every participant’s durable prepare before advancing watermarks. Can you walk me through its ordering?

First, an acknowledgment must pass the epoch fence before recovery can rely on it; a stale acknowledgment cannot be treated as current evidence of preparation. Recovery then uses the replicated transaction decisions to determine which transactions it must account for. Before advancing a visibility watermark for a transaction, it verifies that every participant has a durable prepare capable of supporting that decision.

The plan separates a recorded decision from permission to expose its effects. It describes the required checks and ordering, not an implemented recovery protocol or a measured outcome.
Why fence the prepare acknowledgments specifically?

An acknowledgment is evidence that a participant prepared its part of a transaction. If recovery could reuse an acknowledgment that is stale for the current epoch, it might advance a watermark without valid evidence for every participant. Fencing by epoch makes the acknowledgment’s validity part of the visibility decision, rather than treating any surviving acknowledgment as sufficient.

The plan does not specify how epochs are represented or how an acknowledgment is checked against one.
Does “stale” just mean the acknowledgment is old?

Not simply old in elapsed time. In this plan, staleness is assessed by epoch: the question is whether the acknowledgment remains valid for the leadership context in which recovery would use it. The plan calls for fencing stale acknowledgments; it does not set a time limit or say that every acknowledgment originating before a leader transfer must be discarded regardless of validation.
What information does recovering from replicated decisions give us?

It gives recovery a surviving account of transaction outcomes to consider. A participant’s staged work alone does not say whether its transaction should become visible, and an acknowledgment alone does not substitute for a transaction decision. Replicated decisions provide the outcome side of that distinction; checking every participant’s durable prepare supplies the supporting-work side before a watermark advances.

The plan does not describe the format of the decisions or the procedure used to replay them.
If a commit decision is replicated, why not advance the watermark immediately?

Because the decision by itself does not demonstrate that every participant can supply its required transaction effect after recovery. The plan explicitly puts verification of every participant’s durable prepare before watermark advancement. Otherwise, the watermark could announce a committed snapshot that cannot be presented consistently across the participants.

This is especially important for a multi-shard retraction: its committed visibility must not depend on which shard happens to recover first.
What does verifying a durable prepare need to establish, conceptually?

It needs to establish that the participant’s required prepared work is durable enough to be honored across the failure, rather than merely that an acknowledgment record exists. The epoch fence also has to prevent stale acknowledgment evidence from standing in for that verification. Together, those checks support the decision before it is reflected in an advanced visibility watermark.

The plan does not say which records are inspected or how durability is demonstrated.
Does the check apply only to the participant that had the retracted base row?

No. The plan says *every participant*. For a transaction with effects at multiple participants, checking only the participant holding one base-row retraction would leave the remaining required work unverified. The visibility boundary must be supported by all participants in that transaction.

The plan does not define how participants are enumerated or where particular outer-join and aggregate effects reside.
Suppose three participants are involved and durable preparation can be verified for only two. What happens to the watermark under this plan?

It must not advance to expose that transaction on the strength of those two verifications alone. The plan requires verification of every participant’s durable prepare *before* watermark advancement. Three participants is just an illustration of that all-participants condition, not a specified transaction size.

The plan does not prescribe how recovery obtains the missing verification or what eventual outcome it reaches.
Could recovery still work on that transaction while its watermark remains unchanged?

Yes, as a conceptual distinction: recovering information and exposing a committed snapshot are not the same act. The plan calls for recovering transactions from replicated decisions and checking their participants before advancing watermarks. Internal recovery work therefore should not be mistaken for committed visibility.

It does not specify what other work may proceed while a particular transaction awaits verification.
What if a participant has staged MVCC deltas but its prepare acknowledgment is stale?

The staged deltas do not make the stale acknowledgment valid. Recovery must apply the epoch fence and verify that participant’s durable prepare before the transaction can be included by a watermark advance. The presence of staged work is relevant to recovery, but it is not, by itself, authority to publish the transaction.

Whether and how the existing staged work can be validated is left open by the plan.
Conversely, what if an acknowledgment passes the epoch check but the participant’s prepare is not durable?

Then the plan’s second condition has not been met. Acknowledgment validity and durable preparation are related checks, not interchangeable ones. A watermark should not advance for that transaction until every participant’s durable prepare has been verified.

The plan does not state that passing an epoch check automatically proves durability.
How does this keep a multi-shard retraction from appearing in pieces after failover?

It places an all-participants check before the common visibility boundary advances. Recovery uses the replicated decision, rejects stale acknowledgment evidence through the epoch fence, and verifies each participant’s durable prepare. Only then does the plan permit a watermark advance that could expose the transaction as committed.

That is the intended protection against publishing one shard’s retraction while another participant’s required effect cannot be supported. It remains a plan, not an observation that the protection has succeeded.
Do outer-join match-count changes and aggregate deltas matter to that all-participants check?

They matter to what the transaction’s complete maintained-view effect must represent. A retraction might change whether an outer-join row has a match and alter aggregate contributions. Advancing a watermark while a participant needed for those effects lacks a verified durable prepare could expose an incomplete snapshot.

The plan does not assign match counts or deltas to particular participants, nor does it establish that their values have been computed correctly. Its stated check is that every participant’s prepare is durable before visibility advances.
Does verifying the prepares prove the outer-join and aggregate values themselves match full recomputation?

No. The check concerns whether the required prepared transaction work can support a coherent visibility decision across recovery. A durably prepared delta could still have an incorrect value. Matching full recomputation at every committed snapshot remains a broader correctness requirement, distinct from preventing a watermark from advancing on unverified or stale preparation evidence.
What about a transaction whose replicated decision is available but whose participants have not all been checked yet?

The replicated decision can guide recovery, but it cannot stand in for the missing participant checks. Under this plan, the watermark waits until every participant’s durable prepare is verified. Availability of a decision and readiness for committed visibility are deliberately different conditions.
Is the plan saying to replay every surviving prepare acknowledgment after failover?

No. It says to fence *stale* prepare acknowledgments by epoch and recover transactions from *replicated decisions*. An acknowledgment may be considered only under the epoch-validity and durable-prepare checks; the plan does not instruct recovery to accept every surviving acknowledgment or define a procedure for replaying acknowledgment records.
Does this plan require pausing all writers while recovery verifies a participant?

It does not call for a global writer pause. Its rule is about when a visibility watermark may advance for a transaction whose participants require verification. The broader design requires atomic multi-table updates without globally pausing writers, but this plan alone does not specify which concurrent work can continue during recovery or demonstrate a progress guarantee.
Can the plan be described as avoiding rescans of unaffected base-table partitions?

Not on this statement alone. It specifies epoch fencing, recovery from replicated decisions, participant-level durable-prepare verification, and the condition for advancing watermarks. It does not describe a base-table scanning procedure. The requirement to avoid rescanning unaffected partitions still applies, but this recovery plan does not itself establish how that requirement is met.
Can you state the essential rule without turning the plan into a claim of success?

“Fence stale prepare acknowledgments by epoch; after failover, recover transactions from replicated decisions and verify every participant’s durable prepare before advancing a visibility watermark.” That states the proposed recovery and publication ordering without asserting that it has been implemented or has eliminated partial snapshots.

The next activity is to patch CommitBarrier v1 with epoch-fenced acknowledgments and recovery prepare checks, then rerun LeaderTransfer100K and count partially visible snapshots. What should the patch and rerun establish?

The patch should make acknowledgment validity and recoverable preparation explicit conditions of visibility after leader transfer. An acknowledgment must satisfy its epoch fence, and recovery must check the required durable prepares before a commit barrier advances a visibility watermark. The LeaderTransfer100K rerun then checks the observable outcome by counting committed snapshots that expose only part of a transaction’s required effects.

That is the activity and its intended measurement. No result from the patched rerun has been supplied.
Does patching CommitBarrier v1 mean redesigning all of its staged MVCC deltas?

Not as stated. The named changes are epoch-fenced acknowledgments and recovery prepare checks. CommitBarrier v1 is the artifact being patched; the activity does not say to change the representation of shard-local staged MVCC deltas or to add a new view-computation method.

The relevant connection is that staged effects must not become partly visible on the strength of acknowledgment evidence that recovery has not validated.
What should the epoch fence prevent during the rerun?

It should prevent a prepare acknowledgment from being accepted as valid for a leadership epoch to which it does not apply. Across a leader transfer, the existence of an acknowledgment is not by itself enough to justify making the associated transaction visible. The patch calls for an epoch-based validity check before that acknowledgment can support publication.

The activity does not specify how epochs are represented or the rule for validating a particular acknowledgment.
Are the recovery prepare checks just another way to check the acknowledgment’s epoch?

No. They address a separate question: whether the participants’ required prepared work is durably available to support the transaction after recovery. An acknowledgment might satisfy an epoch check without that fact alone establishing every participant’s durable prepare. The patch names both protections so recovery does not advance visibility on an incomplete basis.

The activity does not specify the records or operations used to perform those checks.
Why do those checks need to happen before advancing a visibility watermark?

The watermark is the committed-visibility boundary. If it advances before the required participant work is verified, a reader could be directed to a snapshot whose transaction effects cannot all be presented. Checking preparation first is intended to keep a retraction and its required derived effects either outside that boundary or visible together.

That describes what the patch is meant to enforce, not a claim that the patched implementation has already done so.
Suppose recovery finds a replicated transaction decision but cannot yet verify one participant’s durable prepare. What is the relevant behavior to test?

The decision alone must not cause a committed snapshot to expose only the participants that recovery has verified. The relevant check is whether the transaction stays out of committed visibility until the required preparation checks support a coherent watermark advance.

The activity does not say how recovery resolves an unverified prepare or how long that takes. The rerun measures whether any partial snapshot becomes visible while such conditions are exercised.
Should the rerun count transactions that have staged work on only some shards?

Not as the specified outcome. Its count is *partially visible snapshots*. Uneven internal staging among shards is not itself partial committed visibility. A snapshot belongs in the count if a committed reader could observe an incomplete set of a transaction’s required effects.

Keep that unit of measurement distinct from numbers of staged transactions, affected shards, acknowledgments, or leader transfers.
Could a snapshot be partial because the base retraction and an outer-join change become visible at different boundaries?

Yes. A retraction may affect whether an outer-join row has a match and may change aggregate contributions. If a committed snapshot exposes the base retraction but not a required derived effect, or exposes the derived effect without the corresponding transaction state, that is the kind of incomplete visibility the count is intended to detect.

The rerun’s partial-snapshot count does not, on its own, verify the arithmetic of every aggregate or the correctness of every computed join row.
Does idempotent failover replay make the recovery prepare checks unnecessary?

No. Idempotence addresses repeated replay without duplicating an effect. Prepare checks address whether the required participant work is durably present before the watermark exposes the transaction. Avoiding duplication does not establish that no participant’s effect is missing.

The activity specifically adds recovery prepare checks to CommitBarrier v1; it does not replace them with replay idempotence.
When I say “rerun LeaderTransfer100K,” how much of its workload can I describe without inventing details?

You can identify it as the leader-transfer stress test involving 100,000 concurrent retraction transactions and leader-transfer crashes, with partially visible snapshots as the measured count. The activity does not supply a number of crashes, a transaction schedule, or a list of crash timings. Those should not be asserted as properties of the rerun.
Would checking only the recovered final view answer the question?

No. The rerun counts partially visible *snapshots*, including committed states that may be exposed while transactions and leader transfers are in progress. A final coherent view would not show whether a reader could previously have seen only part of a retraction. The check needs to attend to committed visibility over the run rather than only its endpoint.
What outcome is this rerun intended to test, and what outcome can we actually report now?

It is intended to test whether the patched acknowledgment fencing and recovery prepare checks prevent partially visible snapshots during LeaderTransfer100K. The measurement is a count of those snapshots. Right now, the node supplies the patch-and-rerun activity, not its observations, so no count for the rerun can be reported.
If that count turned out to be zero, would it demonstrate the entire incremental view maintenance goal?

It would be an observation about atomic visibility under the rerun’s tested leader-transfer workload. It would not, by itself, show that every outer join and aggregate matches full recomputation at every committed snapshot, or establish that writers were never globally paused or unaffected base-table partitions were never rescanned. Those are broader requirements than this partial-snapshot count.

Zero is only a possible result here; the activity has not reported it.
How should I state the activity in one sentence without making the rerun sound completed?
“Patch CommitBarrier v1 with epoch-fenced prepare acknowledgments and recovery prepare checks, then rerun LeaderTransfer100K and count partially visible committed snapshots.”
LeaderTransfer100K still found 2 partial snapshots: recovery advanced watermarks before lagging shards replayed prepared deltas. How should I state the finding?

“LeaderTransfer100K still found 2 partial snapshots: recovery advanced watermarks before lagging shards replayed prepared deltas.” That preserves the observed count, its unit—snapshots—and the reported recovery ordering. It does not turn the finding into a count of affected transactions, shards, or crashes.
What is the essential ordering problem in that sentence?

The visibility watermarks advanced before lagging shards had replayed their prepared deltas. A watermark can make a committed snapshot visible, but that snapshot needs the required shard effects to be present. The finding reports 2 partial snapshots where those steps occurred in the wrong order for complete visibility.
Does “prepared deltas” mean the lagging shards had already made their effects visible?

No. Preparation and replay are distinct from committed visibility. The finding specifically says the lagging shards had not yet replayed the prepared deltas when recovery advanced the watermarks. It does not provide further detail about how the deltas were stored or exactly when each shard later completed replay.
Why can advancing a watermark too early produce a partial snapshot?

A watermark tells committed readers which transaction effects they may treat as visible. If it moves ahead while a required shard has not replayed its prepared delta, the announced snapshot can get ahead of the state available from that shard. The result may expose some of a transaction’s effects without the complete set required at that snapshot. LeaderTransfer100K reports 2 partial snapshots associated with precisely that ordering.
Is this saying the transaction decisions were missing after recovery?

No. The finding identifies premature watermark advancement relative to replay on lagging shards. It does not say that transaction decisions were missing, nor does it describe the contents of the recovered decisions. The narrow reported issue is that committed visibility advanced before the prepared deltas had been replayed where needed.
Can I infer that the prepare acknowledgments were stale?

Not from this finding. It reports that lagging shards had not replayed prepared deltas before recovery advanced watermarks. It does not characterize any acknowledgment as stale or say how acknowledgment checks behaved. An acknowledgment’s validity and completion of replay are different questions; the observation here concerns the latter’s ordering relative to visibility.
So even if recovery can identify a prepared delta, that is different from having replayed it?

Yes. Knowing that prepared work exists does not mean its effect is already available in the recovered state a committed reader needs. The finding makes that distinction concrete: the deltas were described as prepared, yet the lagging shards had not replayed them before the watermarks advanced. It does not specify the mechanism for deciding when replay is complete.
What does “lagging shards” tell me, and what does it leave open?

It tells you that some shards’ replay had not caught up to the watermark advancement. It does not give the number of lagging shards, identify them, or say how long they lagged. The reported count of 2 belongs to partial snapshots, not to shards.
Could I describe the result as 2 partially visible transactions?

No. LeaderTransfer100K found 2 *partial snapshots*. The statement does not establish how many transactions contributed to either snapshot. Keep the observed unit as snapshots rather than converting it into a transaction count.
Do the 2 snapshots tell us how many leader-transfer crashes occurred?
No. The finding names LeaderTransfer100K and describes recovery behavior, but supplies no crash count. Two partial snapshots must not be read as two crashes or two failovers.
Does this observation concern only temporary internal shard state, or something readers could see?

It concerns partial *snapshots*, so the issue is committed visibility, not merely different internal rates of recovery. Shards can be at different stages of replay without that difference itself being a partial committed snapshot. The reported problem is that watermarks advanced while lagging shards had not replayed prepared deltas, and 2 partial snapshots were found.
If the lagging shards replayed their deltas later, would that remove the earlier observation?

No. Later replay might change what a later snapshot presents, but it would not undo an earlier partial snapshot that was already observed. The finding is about visibility at the time those 2 snapshots were exposed; it does not state what later snapshots showed.
What does this finding establish about the relationship between a visibility watermark and replay?

For the observed cases, advancing the watermark before lagging shards replayed prepared deltas was associated with partial snapshots. The practical distinction is that a decision to expose a committed snapshot must not be confused with completion of the effects that snapshot requires. The finding reports the ordering and its observed outcome, without specifying a new publication rule or recovery implementation.
Can I say every outer join and aggregate in those snapshots was wrong?

No. “Partial snapshots” reports incomplete committed visibility, but the finding does not enumerate which outer-join rows, match counts, or aggregate values were affected. Nor does it provide a full-recomputation comparison for every view value. The precise claim is the 2 partial snapshots and the stated replay-versus-watermark ordering.
What if I describe the lagging shards as having lost their prepared deltas?

That would go beyond the finding. It says the shards had not *replayed* their prepared deltas before the watermarks advanced, not that those deltas had been lost. Preserving that distinction matters: a delta may be prepared and yet not be reflected in the recovered state when visibility advances.
Is the number 100,000 the count of partial-snapshot checks or the count of transactions?

LeaderTransfer100K is the named test involving 100,000 transactions. The observation reported here is 2 partial snapshots. The finding does not say how many individual snapshot checks were performed, so 100,000 should not be relabeled as a snapshot-check count.
Can you give me a compact interpretation that stays with the observed result?

LeaderTransfer100K still found 2 partial snapshots because recovery advanced visibility watermarks before lagging shards replayed prepared deltas. The result identifies an observed visibility and replay-ordering problem; it does not specify the number of affected transactions or shards, or report the correctness of every other snapshot.

I want to extend CommitBarrier v1 recovery to await every participant’s replay-applied acknowledgment before publishing watermarks, then rerun LeaderTransfer100K against full recomputation. Can you unpack the activity?

The recovery change adds a publication condition: a watermark must wait until every participant has acknowledged that its prepared transaction effects have actually been applied by replay. The LeaderTransfer100K rerun then compares the maintained view with full recomputation, using the base-table state of the same committed snapshot as the reference.

This is an implementation-and-rerun activity, not a reported outcome. It does not yet say what the comparison finds.
What does “replay-applied acknowledgment” establish that a durable prepare does not?

A durable prepare establishes that the participant has recoverable work for the transaction. A replay-applied acknowledgment establishes a later condition: that the participant has applied the relevant prepared effects during recovery. Suppose a multi-table transaction affects several participants, and one has not provided an applicable certificate. What does the proposal imply?

The snapshot must not be published on the assumption that this participant’s required effects have been applied. Evidence from the others cannot stand in for its missing applicable evidence. The proposal does not define how participants are enumerated, how certificates are collected, or how long publication waits; those are details needed to turn the publication prerequisite into an implementation.
What if a participant presents a certificate with the right transaction digest but the wrong generation?

The generation fence means it cannot simply be counted as valid for publication in the incompatible generation. Correct transaction identity alone is insufficient. The proposal does not prescribe whether the effect must be replayed, recertified, or handled some other way; it only calls for generation-fenced application evidence before publishing the snapshot.
And if it has the right generation but names a different transaction digest?

That certificate does not attest to application of the transaction whose snapshot effects are about to be published. Matching the generation cannot compensate for a different transaction identity. Both the digest binding and the generation fence must be respected for the certificate to serve its proposed purpose.
Does the certificate itself publish any part of the transaction?

No. The proposal distinguishes obtaining an apply certificate from publishing a snapshot. A participant can have applied work and produced applicable evidence without that alone making its portion visible as a committed view. Publication is the separate boundary at which the transaction’s required effects can be exposed coherently.
How do per-key outer-join counts help when a right-side match is retracted?

For an outer join, whether a relevant key has zero matches matters. Retracting one match when others remain removes that matched contribution but does not call for the null-extended result solely because of that retraction. Retracting the last match can also change whether a null-extended result belongs in the view. A per-key match count provides the state needed to distinguish those cases at the snapshot being maintained.

The proposal does not specify the physical representation of a count or every join shape it must support.
Is the only interesting count transition from one to zero?

No. Crossing between zero and nonzero is especially important for the outer-join null-extended result, in either direction. Changes between positive counts also affect which matched results exist. The maintained counts need to support the applicable join changes; the signed aggregate deltas then reflect how those changes affect aggregate contributions.
Can you illustrate the relationship between a count transition and a signed aggregate delta without assuming a particular aggregate?

Consider a left row whose final match is retracted. The matched join result ceases to contribute, and a null-extended join result may become applicable. A dependent aggregate must remove whatever contribution belonged to the former result and account for whatever contribution, if any, belongs to the new one. Signed deltas express that removal and addition, while the count helps determine which join results apply.

The actual contributions depend on the aggregate expression; the proposal does not select one.
Does “signed” mean an aggregate can always be maintained by one simple subtraction?

No. It names the use of positive and negative changes to represent added and retracted contributions. It does not assert that every aggregate has a trivial inverse or specify any auxiliary state that a particular aggregate might require. The maintained aggregate still has to yield the value full recomputation would produce for each committed snapshot.
Should the per-key count and aggregate deltas be associated with the same transaction as the apply certificate?

They need to be coherent with the transaction whose effects are published. If a count reflects one transaction state while the aggregate deltas or application evidence refer to another, the published view could combine incompatible effects. Transaction-digest binding is proposed to keep publication evidence specific; the design would still have to ensure the derived changes it certifies are the ones required for that transaction.
What does the proposal say about a crash between application and snapshot publication?

Application may have occurred without the snapshot yet being published. The distinction must survive recovery: applied work must not become independently visible merely because a certificate exists, and publication must not rely on application evidence invalid for the relevant generation or transaction digest. The proposal names those safeguards but does not specify how certificates or publication state are persisted and recovered.
Could the same signed delta be applied twice during replay and still be covered by a valid-looking certificate?

A certificate is not, by itself, an idempotence mechanism. Applying a signed delta twice could make the maintained value wrong even if publication evidence names the right transaction. A complete design would need application and replay semantics consistent with applying each transaction’s required effect correctly, while the digest-bound certificate and generation fence govern what evidence may support publication. No deduplication procedure is specified in this proposal.
Does this approach require globally pausing writers while certificates are collected?

No such pause is proposed. Waiting to publish a snapshot until its required application evidence is available is conceptually different from globally stopping writers. The design target still requires atomic multi-table updates without globally pausing writers. The proposal does not yet establish the progress behavior of a particular implementation while publication waits.
Can the counts and signed deltas help avoid rescanning unaffected base-table partitions?

That is their intended incremental role: keep information about relevant match states and express the changes to aggregate contributions, rather than recomputing the whole view as the update procedure. The proposal would still need to show that it identifies affected keys and required contributions without rescanning unaffected base-table partitions. Full recomputation remains the reference for correctness, not permission to perform those rescans in maintenance.
What would I compare to tell whether this proposal meets the snapshot-consistency goal?

At each committed snapshot in the required 100,000-transaction scope, including crash recovery, compare the maintained outer-join and aggregate results with full recomputation from the base tables at that same snapshot. Also examine whether a published snapshot ever exposes only a subset of a multi-table transaction’s required effects. The certificates are proposed publication evidence; the counts and deltas are proposed maintenance state. Naming them does not itself establish either observed result.
Is zero partial visibility enough if an outer-join count was computed incorrectly?

No. A transaction could become visible atomically but still carry a wrong match count, joined result, or aggregate contribution. Conversely, correct derived changes could be exposed at an inconsistent boundary. The proposal must support both correct computation and coherent publication to meet the full-recomputation requirement at every committed snapshot.
Can you state the proposal in one sentence that keeps all four ideas and does not present them as proven?

“Use transaction-digest-bound, generation-fenced apply certificates as prerequisites for snapshot publication, while maintaining per-key outer-join match counts and signed aggregate deltas for incremental view changes.” That states the proposed mechanism without asserting that its correctness or operational constraints have already been verified.
How can publication reject superseded replay acknowledgments when leaders transfer repeatedly during a transaction’s recovery?

The proposed approach is to make application evidence specific to both a transaction digest and a leadership generation. Before publishing a snapshot, the barrier would check that each required participant’s apply certificate names the transaction being published and is valid for the generation governing that publication. A replay acknowledgment from a superseded generation must not satisfy the newer barrier merely because it concerns the same transaction.

Repeated transfers make the check important at the moment of publication, not only when an acknowledgment first arrives. This describes the intended validity rule; the proposal does not specify how generations, certificates, or the final publication check are implemented.
Why isn’t matching the transaction digest enough?

The digest answers *which transaction* the evidence concerns. It does not answer whether that evidence remains valid for the leadership context in which the barrier is about to publish a snapshot. An acknowledgment could name the right transaction yet come from a generation that has since been superseded. The generation fence addresses that separate question.
Suppose an acknowledgment arrives while its generation is current, but another leader transfer happens before the watermark is published. Can the earlier check stand?

It cannot simply be assumed to stand. If publication relies only on validity checked at arrival, a later transfer could leave the barrier using evidence from a superseded generation. The publication condition needs to respect the generation applicable when the snapshot becomes visible, including any transfer that occurred while recovery was still in progress.

The proposal does not prescribe a specific way to make that check and publication coherent. It does require that an intervening transfer not silently turn superseded evidence into authorization for a newer barrier.
Does that mean a transfer invalidates all work that was already replayed?

No. Validity of an acknowledgment for a barrier is different from whether replayed work exists. A transfer need not imply that previously applied effects vanish. But publication cannot infer from an acknowledgment belonging to a superseded generation that every required effect is available under the newer publication boundary.

Whether earlier work can be checked again and certified for the newer generation is an implementation question the proposal leaves open. It must not be accepted automatically as though the generations were interchangeable.
What should a newer barrier do if it finds certificates from several generations?

It should not count them together merely to reach the required number of participant acknowledgments. Each certificate used to authorize publication must be valid for that barrier’s generation and bound to the transaction digest it is publishing. A certificate from a superseded generation cannot fill a missing current-generation requirement just because it names a required participant.

The proposal does not say whether such a certificate is discarded, retained for recovery, or used as input to further validation. Rejection *as publication authority* is the key point.
Is the requirement one certificate per shard in the whole system?

No. Publication needs applicable evidence from the participants whose effects are required for the transaction’s snapshot. An unrelated shard does not become a participant merely because it exists. Conversely, a participant responsible for a required derived-view effect cannot be omitted simply because it does not hold the retracted base row.

The proposal does not define how the participant set is identified.
What if every required participant supplies a certificate, but one certificate names a different transaction digest?

The barrier must not treat that as complete evidence for the transaction being published. A matching generation cannot compensate for a mismatched digest: that participant has not supplied an applicable certificate for this transaction. Publication must wait rather than count an acknowledgment for different work toward the required set.
And if all the digests match, but one participant’s certificate is from a superseded generation?

That is still an incomplete set of applicable publication evidence. The digest check establishes transaction identity; the generation check establishes whether the evidence may satisfy this barrier. Both conditions matter for each required participant. The proposal does not dictate how the missing applicable evidence is obtained.
Could the recovering leader just use the most recent acknowledgment it has for each participant?

“Most recent” by arrival time is not enough. A delayed acknowledgment from a superseded generation might arrive after a newer one, and an acknowledgment might concern a different transaction digest. The proposed acceptance condition is validity for the publication generation and the specific transaction, not whichever message happened to arrive last.

This is a conceptual distinction, not a claim about a particular message order in an implementation.
What does an apply certificate need to attest to for a retraction?

To support publication, its application claim needs to cover the required effects for which that participant is responsible—not merely receipt of the transaction or the existence of a durable prepare. A retraction may affect an outer-join match count, a joined result, and an aggregate contribution. Publication must not count a certificate that leaves required participant work unapplied.

The proposal does not specify the exact certificate contents or assign those effects to particular participants. Binding and fencing the certificate also do not, by themselves, prove that the computed deltas have the correct values.
How do the per-key counts and signed aggregate deltas relate to this rejection rule?

They describe the view changes that must remain coherent with the published transaction. Per-key match counts help determine whether a retraction removes one of several matches or the last match, and signed aggregate deltas represent added and removed contributions. The certificate checks govern whether application evidence for those required effects can authorize publication.

A generation-valid certificate cannot repair an incorrect count or delta. Equally, correct counts and deltas must not be exposed through a barrier satisfied by superseded acknowledgments.
If leaders transfer twice while one participant is replaying, must publication accept whichever generation that participant started in?

No. The starting generation does not automatically determine which evidence is valid for eventual publication. The barrier has to evaluate the certificate against the generation governing the snapshot it would publish. Multiple transfers cannot be handled by assuming that an acknowledgment valid at the beginning of replay remains valid for every subsequent barrier.

The proposal leaves open how a participant establishes applicable evidence after those transfers; it only rules out treating superseded evidence as sufficient without the required generation check.
Could an earlier-generation application ever be reused without replaying the delta again?

The proposal does not settle that. Reapplying a signed delta unnecessarily could itself produce an incorrect value, so rejecting an old acknowledgment as publication authority should not be confused with automatically replaying its effects again. A design might establish fresh, generation-valid evidence for already applied work, but it would need to verify that the effects are present and that the certificate meets the transaction-digest and generation conditions. No such recertification procedure is specified here.
Should publication check the generation once per transaction, or once per participant certificate?

Checking only a transaction-level generation label would not establish that *each* certificate being counted is applicable. The intended rule is that every required participant’s evidence used by the barrier is bound to the correct transaction digest and passes the relevant generation fence. The publication decision must then remain coherent with those checks even if leadership changes while it is being made.

That states a correctness condition, not a chosen data structure or coordination protocol.
What if a leader transfer occurs just as all certificates appear to be valid?

That is the boundary the design must handle without a gap between checking certificates and exposing the snapshot. Publication must either be valid under the generation it actually uses or refrain from advancing on evidence that the transfer has superseded. Otherwise, a check that was true just beforehand could be used to authorize a newer barrier for which it is no longer sufficient.

The question calls for that safety condition; it does not supply the atomic procedure for implementing it.
Does withholding the watermark mean readers have to see partially replayed work while they wait?

No. Partially replayed work can remain internal while committed readers continue to use a visibility boundary that does not include the transaction. Withholding publication is meant to prevent a mixture of applied and unapplied effects from being presented as a committed snapshot. Different participants can make recovery progress at different times without those intermediate states becoming visible.
Does the same rule apply if a transaction changes several base tables?

Yes. A multi-table transaction must not be published on the strength of applicable evidence for only some required participants. Its retractions and the dependent outer-join and aggregate changes need to appear at one coherent committed-snapshot boundary. Digest binding helps keep evidence attached to that transaction, while generation fencing prevents superseded evidence from satisfying a later barrier.
Would rejecting old acknowledgments require globally pausing writers?

Not as a logical requirement. The publication boundary for a transaction can wait for applicable evidence without globally pausing writers. The design goal still requires atomic multi-table updates without such a pause, but the certificate proposal alone does not establish what progress a particular implementation achieves while a barrier waits.
And can the certificate checks tell us whether unaffected base-table partitions were rescanned?

No. Certificate validity concerns application evidence and snapshot publication. Per-key counts and signed deltas are proposed for incremental maintenance, but the certificate checks do not measure which base-table partitions the maintenance path reads. Avoiding rescans of unaffected partitions remains a separate requirement.
What would be the simplest invariant to use when reviewing repeated-transfer cases?

At the instant a snapshot is published, every required participant must have applicable evidence that its transaction effects were applied: the evidence must identify the transaction by digest and satisfy the generation fence for that publication. Acknowledgments from superseded generations must not be counted toward a newer barrier merely because they survived another transfer.

That invariant describes what publication must reject or await; it does not assert that a particular implementation already enforces it.

Here is the plan: bind apply certificates to a transaction digest and shard generation; regenerate them after failover, and publish only with each shard’s current-generation certificate. Can you walk through that sequence?

For a transaction being recovered, each required shard’s apply certificate would identify both the transaction digest and that shard’s generation. After failover, the plan is to regenerate the certificate rather than let a certificate from a superseded generation satisfy the publication condition. Snapshot publication waits until each required shard has a certificate for the transaction in its current generation.

That is the proposed ordering and acceptance rule. It does not specify how certificates are produced, how regeneration verifies application, or how the final publication step is implemented.
Why bind the certificate to both values?

The transaction digest answers which transaction’s applied effects the certificate concerns. The shard generation answers whether that shard’s evidence belongs to its current failover context. Matching only the digest could admit evidence from a superseded generation; matching only the generation could admit evidence for a different transaction. The plan requires both checks before that certificate can support publication.
Does “shard generation” mean all shards have to share one generation number?

No shared generation number is specified. The wording binds each certificate to a *shard* generation, and publication requires that shard’s current-generation certificate. The important comparison is between a certificate and the current generation of the shard it represents. The plan does not define how generations are assigned or coordinated across shards.
What happens to a certificate that names the correct transaction digest but belongs to a superseded shard generation?

It cannot satisfy the stated publication condition. After failover, the plan calls for a regenerated certificate, and publication requires a current-generation certificate from that shard. The older certificate might still exist as a record, but its existence is not enough to authorize snapshot publication. The plan does not specify whether or how older records are retained.
If the generation matches but the digest does not, can publication count that certificate?

No. It certifies application associated with a different transaction digest, not the transaction whose effects are being published. Current-generation status cannot substitute for transaction identity. Each certificate counted toward publication must satisfy both bindings.
Does regenerating a certificate after failover mean applying its signed aggregate delta again?

Not necessarily. Regenerating *evidence of application* is distinct from applying the underlying effect a second time. Applying a signed delta twice could make an aggregate incorrect. The plan calls for a new certificate after failover, but does not say whether the shard verifies already-applied work, replays work that remains unapplied, or follows another procedure before issuing it. In every case, a certificate used for publication must truthfully attest to the required application.
Could a shard just change the generation field on an old certificate?

Changing the field alone would not establish that the certificate is valid evidence of application in the current generation. “Regenerate after failover” calls for a current-generation certificate, not merely a relabeled superseded one. The plan does not prescribe the validation steps needed to produce that certificate, so it should not be described as allowing a field change to stand in for them.
Why require the certificate to attest to application rather than just durable preparation?

Durable preparation means the work can be available for recovery; application means the effects needed for the published snapshot have been applied. Publication could get ahead of a shard that has prepared work but has not yet made its required effects available. An apply certificate is meant to provide evidence for that later condition, bound to the transaction and the shard’s current generation.
Suppose a transaction affects two shards. One has a current-generation certificate, but the other has only a certificate from before failover. What should readers see?

The transaction should not be published on the strength of those certificates. The second shard lacks the current-generation certificate required by the plan. Committed readers must not see a snapshot that exposes only the first shard’s effects while waiting for applicable evidence from the second.

Two shards are just an illustration; the plan does not specify a particular transaction’s participant count.
Does “each shard” mean every shard in the whole system must issue a certificate for every transaction?

Read it in the context of the transaction’s required shard effects: publication needs a current-generation certificate from each shard whose applied effects it relies on. The plan does not say unrelated shards participate in every transaction, and it does not specify how the relevant set of shards is identified. A required shard cannot be omitted just because another shard has already certified its own work.
What if leadership transfers again while certificates are being regenerated?

The current-generation condition still governs publication. A certificate regenerated for a generation that is then superseded must not satisfy publication as though it came from the shard’s new current generation. The shard would need applicable current-generation evidence under the plan before its effects could support publication. Repeated transfers do not make the digest requirement disappear either.
Could the system check the certificates, experience another failover, and then publish on the basis of the earlier check?

That would risk publishing with certificates that are no longer current. The publication decision must respect each required shard’s current generation when the snapshot is published, not merely when certificates were first inspected. The plan states that rule but does not specify an atomic check-and-publication mechanism to enforce it across a concurrent failover.
What if only one shard transfers leadership while another shard retains its generation?

The plan’s check is per shard. The transferring shard needs a certificate for its current generation after failover. A certificate from a shard whose generation remains current is not made superseded merely because a different shard transferred. Both still need certificates bound to the transaction digest before publication. The plan does not prescribe how the system confirms the generation of either shard.
Is a current-generation certificate enough if it covers only the retracted base row and not a required view change?

Not for publishing a snapshot that depends on the missing change. The certificate must substantiate application of the effects required from that shard for the transaction; otherwise, it could be current and digest-bound while still leaving the published view incomplete. The plan does not define the certificate’s detailed coverage or assign particular outer-join and aggregate changes to particular shards.
How do per-key outer-join counts and signed aggregate deltas fit with this plan?

They describe changes that may need to be applied for a retraction: a per-key count can determine whether an outer join loses its last match, and signed deltas can account for removed and added aggregate contributions. The certificate plan concerns whether the required shard effects for that transaction have been applied and can be published together. It does not itself calculate a correct count or delta; those values still have to agree with the committed snapshot.
Could all certificates be valid and the view still differ from full recomputation?

Yes. Valid certificates could show that the effects prepared for a particular transaction were applied in the applicable shard generations, yet a prepared outer-join or aggregate change might have been calculated incorrectly. Certificate validity addresses transaction identity, generation, and application before publication. Full-recomputation equality is a separate correctness condition.
What does this plan say about a transaction whose recovery is still underway on one shard?

Publication waits if that shard cannot yet supply its current-generation apply certificate for the transaction. Internal recovery on other shards can be further along without becoming a partial committed snapshot. The plan sets a safety condition for publication; it does not say how long recovery takes or guarantee that publication eventually occurs.
Would waiting for that shard require stopping writers everywhere?

The plan restricts publication of a snapshot that needs that shard’s certificate; it does not call for globally pausing writers. Whether a particular implementation lets unaffected writers make progress while publication waits is an operational question not answered by the certificate rule alone.
Does this plan say anything about rescanning unaffected base-table partitions?

No. Binding and regenerating apply certificates controls which application evidence can authorize snapshot publication. It does not specify what base-table partitions are read while maintaining outer-join counts or aggregate deltas. The requirement not to rescan unaffected partitions remains distinct from this publication plan.
Can you give me a compact invariant for reviewing repeated failovers?

At snapshot publication, each required shard must supply an apply certificate for the transaction digest that is valid for that shard’s *current* generation. After failover, regenerate the certificate rather than counting evidence from a superseded generation. That states the planned publication rule without claiming it has been implemented or tested.

The activity is to implement digest-bound, generation-fenced apply certificates, then run EpochStorm100K with overlapping failovers and compare outer joins and aggregates against recomputation. Can you separate the implementation work from the test?

The implementation work is to make each apply certificate identify the transaction by digest and carry a shard-generation validity condition. The test is to run EpochStorm100K while failovers overlap and compare the maintained outer-join and aggregate results with full recomputation at corresponding committed snapshots.

Those are actions to perform, not results. The activity supplies no mismatch count or other observation from this run.
What should the digest binding prevent?

It should prevent evidence of application for one transaction from being accepted as evidence for a different transaction. A certificate used to support publication needs to refer to the digest of the transaction whose effects are at issue. The activity does not define the digest format, what data goes into it, or a certificate-verification procedure.
And what should the generation fence prevent?

It should prevent an apply certificate associated with a superseded shard generation from being accepted merely because the certificate still exists. With overlapping failovers, the generation applicable to a shard can change while transaction recovery is underway. The certificate must be valid for the generation in which it is used to support publication.

The activity does not prescribe how generations are assigned or how an implementation makes the validity check coherent with publication.
Why are the digest and the generation separate checks?

They answer separate questions: *which transaction* does the certificate concern, and *for which shard generation* is its application evidence valid? A certificate can name the right transaction yet belong to an inapplicable generation. It can also belong to the applicable generation but name a different transaction. Neither check replaces the other.
Does an apply certificate just mean the shard received a transaction bundle?

No. In this activity, it is application evidence, not merely evidence of receipt or preparation. The distinction matters when a failover interrupts recovery: work may be identified or prepared without its required effects having been applied. The activity does not specify precisely how a shard establishes that application occurred before issuing a certificate.
Should the certificate cover a base-table retraction but leave the dependent view changes for later?

It cannot safely authorize publication of a snapshot that needs dependent changes still missing from the shard’s required work. A retraction may alter an outer-join result and its aggregate contributions. The implementation would need to define the certificate’s coverage so its application claim is appropriate for the effects being published.

This activity does not specify the certificate contents or where particular derived changes are maintained.
What happens to certificate validity if another failover overlaps recovery?

The relevant shard generation must still be checked when the certificate is used. A certificate obtained before another failover must not automatically satisfy a publication condition after its generation has been superseded. The stated implementation work is the digest binding and generation fence; the exact method of obtaining applicable evidence after a subsequent failover is not specified in this activity.
If a shard has applied the transaction, does a new generation necessarily mean applying its aggregate delta again?

No. Establishing application evidence for a generation is distinct from repeating the underlying effect. Applying the same signed aggregate delta twice could make the maintained value incorrect. The activity does not say whether a recovering shard verifies an effect already present, applies an effect still pending, or uses another recovery procedure; the eventual outer-join and aggregate values are what the recomputation comparison will check.
Could a certificate pass both identity checks and the view still be wrong?

Yes. A certificate can correctly identify the transaction and applicable shard generation while the applied outer-join or aggregate delta has an incorrect value. The certificate checks address which application evidence may support publication. Comparing maintained outer joins and aggregates against full recomputation tests the resulting values separately.
How should that recomputation comparison be aligned with snapshots?

Compare each maintained result being checked with a full recomputation from the base-table state of the *same committed snapshot*. Otherwise, a difference could reflect two different transaction states rather than incorrect maintenance. The activity calls for comparison against recomputation but does not specify the number of snapshots compared or a comparison procedure.
Why name both outer joins and aggregates in the test?

They can respond differently to a retraction. An outer join must account for whether a row still has a match, including transitions involving a null-extended result. An aggregate must account for the contributions removed or added by the resulting join change. Comparing both against recomputation tests both kinds of maintained result rather than treating a correct visibility boundary as proof that their values are correct.
Can you give a small conceptual example of the kind of view change the comparison should catch?

For a left row whose last right-side match is retracted, the matched join result ceases to apply and a null-extended result may become applicable. A dependent aggregate may need to remove one contribution and account for another. The maintained join and aggregate at that committed snapshot should equal results recomputed from the base tables at the same snapshot.

That is an illustration of the semantics to compare, not a statement that EpochStorm100K includes a particular row or aggregate expression.
Do per-key match counts and signed aggregate deltas replace the recomputation comparison?

No. They are proposed incremental maintenance state: match counts help identify outer-join transitions, and signed deltas express changes in aggregate contributions. Full recomputation provides an independent reference for the results of those computations. Implementing certificates and using incremental state do not, by themselves, establish equality with that reference.
Does running recomputation as a reference mean the maintenance system is allowed to rescan unaffected base-table partitions for every transaction?

No. Recomputing a reference for the test is separate from incrementally maintaining the view. The design requirement excludes rescanning unaffected base-table partitions in the maintenance path. This activity specifies a correctness comparison; it does not describe or measure which partitions the maintenance path reads.
What exactly is being overlapped in EpochStorm100K?

The activity says *failovers* overlap while EpochStorm100K runs. That exercises certificate validity and maintained results when recovery contexts can change before earlier work is finished. It does not specify how many failovers occur, how many overlap at once, which shards are affected, or their timing.
Can I infer an exact transaction count from the name EpochStorm100K?

The activity gives EpochStorm100K as the run’s name, but does not separately specify a transaction count for this run. Preserve the name without using it to invent a precise number of transactions, comparisons, reads, or failovers.
Should I describe the test as counting partial reads as well?

Not as a stated measurement of this activity. It expressly says to compare outer joins and aggregates against recomputation under overlapping failovers. Partial visibility remains a relevant concern when certificates are used before publication, but this activity supplies no instruction to count partial reads and no resulting count. A recomputation mismatch count should not be silently converted into a partial-read count either.
If the comparison finds zero mismatches, can I say the certificate mechanism is proved correct for all failovers?

No. If a completed run reports zero mismatches, that would describe the snapshots and comparisons exercised in that run. It would not prove behavior for every possible failover schedule or establish every property of the certificate mechanism. At present, even that zero is conditional: the activity states a comparison to perform, not its outcome.
What if the comparison finds a mismatch? Would that necessarily mean the generation fence failed?

Not necessarily. A mismatch could concern an incorrectly computed outer-join transition or aggregate delta even if the certificates were checked as intended. The proposed comparison would establish that a maintained result differs from recomputation; determining why would require information the activity does not provide. No mismatch has been reported here.
Does this activity measure whether writers on unaffected partitions continue at a particular throughput?

No. Its named test checks outer joins and aggregates against recomputation with overlapping failovers. It gives no unaffected-partition throughput target or measurement. Value equality would not, by itself, establish writer progress or the absence of a global writer pause.
