Can you give me a one-sentence description that preserves the exact activity without implying it has succeeded?

“Implement transaction-digest-bound, generation-fenced apply certificates, then run EpochStorm100K with overlapping failovers and compare the maintained outer joins and aggregates against full recomputation at corresponding committed snapshots.”
EpochStorm100K recorded zero partial snapshots and zero recomputation mismatches; untouched partitions required no rescans. How should I state that result without overstating it?

“In EpochStorm100K, zero partial snapshots and zero recomputation mismatches were recorded, and untouched partitions required no rescans.” Keep those as three observations from the run. They concern committed visibility, agreement with the recomputation reference, and scan behavior for untouched partitions, respectively; they are not a guarantee about every possible execution.
Are the two zeros redundant?

No. Zero partial snapshots says the run recorded no committed snapshot exposing an incomplete set of a transaction’s required effects. Zero recomputation mismatches says the maintained results compared in the run did not differ from recomputation. A view can be published as a coherent unit yet contain an incorrect outer-join or aggregate value, so the recomputation finding adds something distinct.
Does “partial snapshots” mean shards could never be at different stages of recovery?

No. Shards can be at different stages internally without exposing those stages as committed snapshots. The reported zero concerns *visible snapshots*, not simultaneous processing or replay at every shard.
What does the recomputation finding tell us about the outer joins and aggregates?

EpochStorm100K compared maintained outer joins and aggregates against recomputation, and the result reports zero mismatches. That is an observation about the maintained values covered by those comparisons. It does not specify how many individual rows or aggregate values were compared, or establish their correctness in executions outside the run.
Can I read the 100K in EpochStorm100K as an exact count of snapshots checked?

No. EpochStorm100K is the test’s name here. The finding gives no separate numerical count of snapshots, transactions, reads, failovers, or comparisons. The exact numerical results supplied are zero partial snapshots and zero recomputation mismatches; the scan result is stated without a numerical partition count.
Does zero recomputation mismatches imply that there were zero failovers?

No. A mismatch count is not a failover count. EpochStorm100K was run with overlapping failovers, but this result does not state how many occurred. The zero says that no mismatch was recorded in the recomputation comparisons.
How should I interpret “untouched partitions required no rescans”?

It means the reported run did not require rescanning partitions untouched by the relevant changes. That is a statement about avoiding *rescans* of untouched partitions, not a claim that no base-table partitions were ever read or that every possible operation involved no scans. The result also gives no count of untouched partitions.
Could I say no partitions were scanned at all?

No. “Untouched partitions required no rescans” does not rule out reading affected data, and it does not describe every scan in the system. Keeping “untouched” and “rescans” in the statement preserves its actual scope.
Is the full recomputation itself a forbidden rescan of an untouched partition?

The recomputation comparison is a correctness reference, whereas the no-rescans observation concerns what the incremental maintenance required for untouched partitions. The result can report both without implying that the maintenance path recomputed the view by scanning untouched partitions. It does not give the mechanics of the test’s reference computation.
Does the scan observation establish that writers on untouched partitions maintained baseline throughput?

No. Avoiding rescans and sustaining a particular writer throughput are different measurements. This EpochStorm100K finding supplies no throughput percentage, baseline comparison, or writer-progress measurement. Its operational observation is specifically that untouched partitions required no rescans.
What can I say about the transaction-digest-bound, generation-fenced apply certificates from this result?

They are the implementation approach exercised in the EpochStorm100K activity. You can describe the result as observations from a run using that approach: zero partial snapshots, zero recomputation mismatches, and no required rescans of untouched partitions. The observations do not by themselves isolate which component produced each outcome or prove that the certificates will behave identically under every failover schedule.
Can I claim that each certificate was valid in every generation encountered?

The reported findings do not include a certificate-by-certificate validity audit. They tell us what was observed in committed snapshots, recomputation comparisons, and untouched-partition rescans. Certificate validity is part of the intended publication mechanism, but this result should not be expanded into a count or description of every certificate checked.
Does zero partial snapshots mean the test checked zero snapshots?

No. Zero is the number of *partial* snapshots recorded, not the number of snapshots examined. The result does not state the total snapshot count, so it would be wrong either to call that total zero or to derive one from the test name.
What if a later execution exposes a partial snapshot? Would that change how I report EpochStorm100K?

It would not change what this run recorded. EpochStorm100K’s stated result remains zero partial snapshots and zero recomputation mismatches, with no rescans required for untouched partitions. A different execution would have its own observations; the present finding should remain bounded to this run rather than being presented as a universal guarantee.
Does the result fully establish the original requirement to match recomputation at every committed snapshot across 100,000 transactions, including crash recovery?

It reports zero recomputation mismatches in EpochStorm100K, which exercised overlapping failovers, but it does not separately state a count of 100,000 transactions or say exactly how many committed snapshots were compared. Nor does it establish a universal result beyond the run. State the finding as reported rather than converting the test name into additional coverage claims.
And does it fully establish atomic multi-table updates without globally pausing writers?

The zero partial-snapshot observation addresses incomplete committed visibility in this run, and the no-rescans observation addresses untouched partitions. Neither reports whether writers were globally paused. The result should not be used to assert an unmeasured writer-progress property.
Can you give me a concise sentence that keeps the visibility, value, and scan observations distinct?
“EpochStorm100K recorded zero partial snapshots and zero outer-join or aggregate recomputation mismatches, while untouched partitions required no rescans.”
Should I attach an exact failover count or throughput figure to that sentence?
No. This finding supplies neither. It identifies the run and its three observations, but not the number of overlapping failovers or a writer-throughput measurement.
What does ApplyCert v1 provide?

ApplyCert v1 provides transaction-digest-bound, generation-fenced shard certificates and a publication gate that verifies all current-generation participants. The certificates tie application evidence to a particular transaction and shard generation; the gate checks the required participants before allowing snapshot publication. That describes the artifact’s capabilities, without specifying its certificate format or publication protocol.
What is the transaction digest doing in a shard certificate?

It binds the certificate to the transaction whose effects are at issue. A certificate for one transaction must not count as evidence for another merely because it came from a required shard. The artifact description does not specify how the digest is computed or what information it covers.
And what is fenced by the generation?

The certificate’s validity as evidence for publication is generation-fenced. A certificate belonging to a superseded shard generation should not satisfy a gate that requires evidence from that shard’s current generation, even if its transaction digest matches. The artifact description does not define how generations are assigned or changed.
So the digest and generation are not two names for the same check?

Right. The digest identifies *which transaction* the certificate concerns. The generation determines whether that shard certificate is applicable in its current context. A certificate can pass one check and fail the other, so the publication gate needs both distinctions.
What does the publication gate verify about the participants?

It verifies all current-generation participants before publication. In practical terms, a certificate from only some required participants is not enough, and a certificate from a required participant must be applicable to its current generation and the transaction being published. The statement does not specify how the participant set is determined or how the checks are carried out.
Does that mean every shard in the distributed system must provide a certificate for each transaction?

No. “All participants” refers to the shards participating in the transaction’s required effects, not automatically every shard in the system. The gate cannot omit a required participant merely because other participants have supplied valid certificates, but the artifact description does not make unrelated shards participants.
If one required shard has a current-generation certificate and another has only an older-generation certificate, can the gate publish?

Not on the basis of those two certificates. The older-generation certificate does not meet the stated current-generation condition for its shard. The first shard’s applicable evidence cannot stand in for the second shard’s missing applicable evidence. The description does not say what procedure supplies a usable certificate for the second shard.
What if both certificates are current-generation, but one has the wrong transaction digest?

That still does not give the gate applicable evidence from every participant for the transaction being published. The certificate with the wrong digest concerns another transaction. Being current for its shard does not make it valid for this transaction’s publication.
Can a certificate itself publish that shard’s part of a transaction?

The artifact describes certificates and a separate publication gate. A certificate is evidence the gate can verify; it is not, by itself, snapshot publication. Keeping those roles separate matters for a transaction whose required effects involve more than one shard.
Does a valid certificate prove that an outer-join count or signed aggregate delta has the right value?

Not from this description alone. Transaction and generation binding concern which application evidence the gate may accept. They do not independently prove the arithmetic of a signed aggregate delta or the correctness of an outer-join match count. Those maintained results still have to satisfy the separate requirement to match full recomputation at the relevant committed snapshot.
Then what does the word “apply” in ApplyCert v1 contribute?

It identifies these as apply certificates: evidence associated with application of a shard’s transaction effects, rather than merely a transaction identifier or a publication marker. The description does not spell out what a shard must do before issuing a certificate or exactly which effects its application claim covers. Those details should not be invented from the artifact name.
Could the gate treat a certificate for a base-row retraction as proof that every dependent view effect has been applied?

It should not assume coverage that the certificate has not established. A retraction can affect an outer join and an aggregate, and a published snapshot needs its required effects to be coherent. ApplyCert v1’s stated bindings and all-participant gate do not specify the detailed coverage of each certificate, so the artifact description alone cannot certify that every dependent value is correct or present.
How should the gate behave if leadership changes while certificates are being collected?

Its stated current-generation check remains relevant. A certificate that was applicable when collected cannot simply be assumed applicable after its shard’s generation has changed. The gate must verify evidence appropriate to the participants’ current generations for the publication it is considering.

ApplyCert v1’s description does not say how the verification and publication steps are coordinated across a simultaneous leadership change.
Does ApplyCert v1 specify that old certificates are deleted after a generation change?

No. Generation fencing limits whether a certificate can satisfy the publication gate; it does not, by itself, specify record deletion or retention. An older certificate might exist without being acceptable evidence for a current-generation participant. The artifact statement makes no storage-policy claim.
Does it specify how a current-generation certificate is obtained after failover?

No. ApplyCert v1 provides generation-fenced shard certificates and a gate that verifies all current-generation participants, but its description does not give a regeneration, replay, or recertification procedure. It would be inaccurate to infer that getting a new certificate necessarily reapplies a transaction’s effects.
If one shard changes generation and the others do not, do all their certificates become invalid?

The generation condition is assessed for each participating shard. A certificate from the shard that changed generation must be appropriate to its new current generation; another shard’s certificate is not made old solely because that first shard changed. Each certificate still needs the correct transaction digest. The description does not specify any broader rule invalidating every participant’s evidence together.
Is collecting one applicable certificate from each participant automatically sufficient to publish?

The stated rule is a gate: publication is conditioned on verification of all current-generation participants. It does not say that this is the only publication condition or that publication occurs immediately upon receipt of the final certificate. Describing it as a prerequisite is more precise than asserting an unspecified complete commit protocol.
What does this artifact contribute to atomic visibility of multi-shard retractions?

It supplies transaction-specific, generation-fenced evidence at each participating shard and an all-participants check before snapshot publication. That is the visibility role of the artifact: publication should not proceed using evidence from only some participants, from a different transaction, or from an inapplicable generation. The feature description alone is not a proof that every execution produces an atomic and correct maintained view.
Does verifying all participants require their internal application steps to happen simultaneously?

No. Participants can reach the point of supplying certificates at different times. The gate concerns what must be verified *before publication*, not whether their internal work occurs at the same instant. Uneven internal progress need not be exposed as a partially applied committed snapshot.
Does ApplyCert v1 say anything about globally pausing writers?

It states a condition on snapshot publication, not a global writer-pause rule. Waiting for applicable certificates from participants does not, by itself, specify what writers on other partitions do while the gate waits. The artifact description therefore should not be presented either as requiring a global pause or as measuring uninterrupted writer progress.
Can the gate establish that unaffected base-table partitions were not rescanned?

No. It verifies certificates before publication; it does not describe which base-table partitions incremental maintenance reads. Avoiding rescans of unaffected partitions is a separate operational property and cannot be inferred from certificate validity alone.
What is a compact description of ApplyCert v1 that stays within what the artifact says?
“ApplyCert v1 provides transaction-digest-bound, generation-fenced shard certificates and gates snapshot publication on verification of all current-generation participants.”
I propose using partitioned MVCC lineage indexes and per-key differential joins to reconcile null-extended rows and aggregates before certified snapshot publication. How do those pieces fit together?

The lineage indexes are proposed to identify the versioned inputs relevant to a change without treating the entire base table as affected. Per-key differential joins then determine how that change alters joined output for the relevant keys. Reconciliation accounts for both matched rows and null-extended outer-join rows, including their aggregate contributions. Only after those derived effects are reconciled should the resulting snapshot be eligible for certified publication.

That describes the proposed division of responsibilities. It does not specify an index layout, a differential-join algorithm, or the procedure that certifies publication.
What does “lineage” mean here?

Conceptually, lineage connects a maintained result to the base-table inputs and versions that contribute to it. When an input changes or is retracted, that connection helps identify which join results and aggregate contributions may need reconsideration. The MVCC aspect matters because those relationships must be interpreted for the committed snapshot being maintained, not against an arbitrary mixture of versions.

The proposal calls for lineage indexes but does not define exactly what entries they contain or how they are updated.
Why make the lineage indexes partitioned?

Partitioning makes it possible, in principle, to locate relevant lineage without looking through unrelated base-table partitions for each change. That is important to the requirement not to rescan unaffected base-table partitions. It does not mean that each transaction is confined to one partition: a transaction can have relevant effects at multiple participants.

The proposal does not choose partition boundaries or prove that every affected lineage entry can be found without an unaffected-partition rescan. Those are properties the eventual design would need to establish.
Does MVCC mean the index has to give the same answer for every concurrent transaction?

No. The relevant answer depends on which versions belong to the committed snapshot under consideration. Concurrent transactions may have work in progress, but a lineage lookup used to maintain or validate one committed snapshot cannot freely combine versions from different transaction states. MVCC is proposed to preserve that distinction while the per-key changes are worked out.
What is differential about the per-key join?

Rather than recomputing the entire join, it considers how changes to inputs for a relevant key alter that key’s joined results. For an insertion, retraction, or other change, the question is which output contributions appear, disappear, or change at the target snapshot. “Per-key” limits the reasoning to the keys implicated by the change, subject to correctly identifying all of them.

The proposal does not prescribe a particular representation for the input changes or the join’s intermediate state.
Why mention null-extended rows explicitly? Wouldn’t an ordinary join delta cover them?

An outer join has output that can exist specifically because no match exists. If the last match for a left-side row is retracted, removing its matched result is not the entire delta: a null-extended result may now belong in the view. When a first match appears, the null-extended result may need to disappear. A differential join that handled only matched row pairs would miss those transitions.

Reconciliation means accounting for the complete outer-join result at the relevant committed snapshot, including that absence-of-match case.
If one of several matches is retracted, should the null-extended row appear?

Not solely because that one match was retracted. If another applicable match remains at the snapshot, the left-side row is still matched. The differential change removes the contribution associated with the retracted match, while the null-extended case depends on whether the relevant match set has become empty. The proposal does not dictate how the implementation determines that emptiness.
And what if a match arrives for a row that was previously null-extended?

Then reconciliation has to account for both sides of the transition: the null-extended result no longer applies, and the newly matched result or results do. Any dependent aggregate must reflect the removal of the former contribution and the addition of the new contribution as appropriate. A snapshot that contains both kinds of result when they are mutually inconsistent, or neither when one is required, would not match full recomputation.
Are null-extended rows necessarily stored as literal rows in the lineage index?

The proposal does not say. “Reconcile null-extended rows” describes the required output behavior, not a required physical representation. An implementation could represent information about absence of matches in different ways, but whatever it does must produce the correct outer-join result for the snapshot being published. No particular storage choice should be inferred from the phrase “lineage indexes.”
How do aggregates enter the same reconciliation step?

An aggregate over the join depends on the joined results that actually exist. If differential processing removes a matched row, introduces a null-extended row, or reverses that transition, the aggregate’s maintained state must reflect the appropriate contributions. Reconciliation is not complete merely because the outer-join rows look right; the aggregate must correspond to those rows at the same snapshot.

The proposal does not name an aggregate expression, so it does not establish a universal arithmetic rule for every aggregate.
Could the join results be correct while the aggregate is still wrong?

Yes. For example, an aggregate might retain a contribution from a matched result after that result has been retracted, or omit a contribution associated with a newly applicable result. Those are conceptual possibilities, not reported observations. The proposal expressly includes aggregates in the work to reconcile before publication so that matching joined rows alone is not treated as sufficient.
Does a per-key differential join have to make every change visible as soon as it computes that key?

No. Computing a key’s change is different from publishing the transaction’s committed snapshot. Other keys, tables, partitions, or aggregate effects required by the same transaction may still need reconciliation. The proposal places certified snapshot publication *after* the null-extended rows and aggregates have been reconciled; it does not make an individual key’s completion an independent visibility boundary.
Suppose a transaction changes two tables. Would separate lineage lookups for the two changes be enough?

They can help identify relevant effects, but the published view still needs the transaction’s combined result. Processing one table’s changes and publishing them before the other table’s required join and aggregate effects are accounted for could expose a state inconsistent with the committed snapshot. The proposal uses lineage and per-key differential work to determine changes, while certified publication remains the boundary for exposing their reconciled outcome.

It does not prescribe how multi-table work is scheduled or bundled.
What if two concurrent transactions affect the same key?

The per-key differential calculations must be interpreted against the appropriate MVCC snapshots, and the published results must respect committed transaction visibility. A calculation based on one transaction’s state cannot silently use another transaction’s effects before they belong to that snapshot. Both transactions may require changes at the same key, but the proposal does not specify an ordering or conflict-resolution protocol for their internal work.
Would a lineage index entry from a different snapshot still be useful?

It might provide information that can be interpreted through MVCC, but it cannot simply be taken as the applicable contributor set for every snapshot. The relevant versions and their lineage must agree with the committed snapshot being maintained. Whether an index stores historical entries, filters them by version, or uses another representation is not specified by the proposal.
How do retractions interact with lineage? Is deleting the index entry always sufficient?

No. A retraction can remove a contribution, change whether other matches remain, cause a null-extended result to become applicable, and change an aggregate. The lineage index helps identify the affected relationships, but removing an index entry alone would not necessarily perform all those derived changes. The index’s own state also has to be interpreted consistently with the snapshot whose join and aggregate results are being reconciled.
Does the word “certified” specify which certification mechanism to use?

Not in this proposal. It says reconciliation should precede *certified snapshot publication*. That makes certification a publication prerequisite, but does not define certificate fields, who issues certificates, or the exact publication protocol. The essential separation is between derived work that may be under way and a snapshot that can be exposed as a coherent committed result.
Could publication be certified if the outer join has been reconciled but an affected aggregate is still pending?

That would not satisfy the ordering proposed here. It expressly places reconciliation of null-extended rows *and aggregates* before certified snapshot publication. Certification for the snapshot cannot be treated as evidence of complete view state if a required aggregate effect is still pending.
How does this approach relate to failures of a partition during recovery?

The maintained output after recovery still has to correspond to a committed MVCC snapshot. If an affected partition has not recovered the lineage or differential effects required for that snapshot, publishing the snapshot as fully reconciled would risk exposing an incomplete outer join or aggregate. Certified publication is intended to follow, not precede, the required reconciliation.

The proposal does not define a failure-recovery algorithm or say how an unavailable partition supplies the necessary state.
If some partitions are unaffected, does certification require recomputing them anyway?

No such recomputation is proposed. Partitioned lineage indexes and per-key differential joins are intended to focus maintenance on relevant changes. The design goal explicitly excludes rescanning unaffected base-table partitions. A complete implementation would still need to show that it can identify every affected contribution and certify the resulting snapshot without falling back to such rescans.
Could a partition be unaffected in its base rows but still hold a derived effect?

That is a distinction the design would need to handle. “Unaffected” cannot be decided solely by whether a base row on a partition changed if a transaction also has a required join or aggregate effect elsewhere. The proposal does not specify placement of derived state, so it does not provide a rule for classifying particular partitions. Its no-rescan aim must coexist with identifying all genuinely affected work.
Does partitioning the lineage index alone prove that unaffected base-table partitions are never rescanned?

No. Partitioning offers a way to localize searches, but the property depends on how affected keys and contributors are identified and how the index is maintained. An index with incomplete or inconsistent lineage could still force a broad scan or produce a wrong result. The proposal supplies a direction for the design, not a measured scan outcome.
Why compare this design to full recomputation if the point is to avoid recomputing?

Full recomputation is the correctness reference. At a committed snapshot, it tells us what the outer join and aggregates should be from that snapshot’s base tables. The incremental path is intended to reach that same result through lineage-guided, per-key changes without rescanning unaffected base-table partitions. Using full recomputation for comparison does not make it the maintenance algorithm.
What exactly is the required scope of that comparison?

The design goal requires matching full recomputation at every committed snapshot across 100,000 transactions, including crash recovery. For each such comparison, the maintained view and recomputed reference must represent the same snapshot. The proposal does not report that this comparison has been carried out or that it has passed.
If all visible results match recomputation, does that show writers were not globally paused?

No. Result equality is about correctness of the exposed view; it does not measure writer progress. The design also requires atomic multi-table updates without globally pausing writers. A lineage-guided maintenance strategy and deferred snapshot publication may be compatible with that requirement, but this proposal does not establish how writers behave while reconciliation or certification waits.
Is certified publication supposed to wait for every key in the system?

The proposed ordering concerns the effects required for the snapshot being published, not a stated obligation to recompute every unrelated key. Per-key differential joins and partitioned lineage indexes are meant to focus on relevant work. The proposal does not define a precise affected-key set or a publication protocol, so it should not be paraphrased as a system-wide key scan.
Can you state a useful correctness invariant for a key whose last match disappears?

At the committed snapshot where that last match is absent, the maintained join should no longer include the retracted matched result and should include the applicable null-extended result. Any aggregate depending on those results should reflect the corresponding change. The lineage and differential work must produce that reconciled state before the snapshot is published; the final output should equal full recomputation at that snapshot.
And if another match still exists at that snapshot?

Then the retracted match’s result ceases to apply, but absence of a match has not been established, so the retraction should not introduce a null-extended result on that basis. Other applicable matched results remain, and the aggregate should reflect the changed set of joined results. That distinction is why the per-key calculation must consider the relevant match state at the target MVCC snapshot.
What would this proposal leave undecided for an implementation?

It leaves the lineage index representation, its partitioning scheme, the exact per-key differential algorithm, the way aggregate state is represented, and the mechanics of certified publication unspecified. Those choices must ultimately support correct snapshot-aligned reconciliation, recovery, and atomic visibility without global writer pauses or rescans of unaffected base-table partitions. None of those implementation choices is established just by naming the proposed components.
Give me a compact statement of the proposal that preserves its ordering.

“Use partitioned MVCC lineage indexes and per-key differential joins to reconcile null-extended outer-join rows and aggregate results, then publish the reconciled snapshot through certification.” The ordering matters: compute and reconcile the required effects before making the snapshot visible.
How can per-key lineage prevent duplicate null-extended rows when concurrent retractions and inserts change join matches within one snapshot?

Per-key lineage can help by identifying the left-side row and all matching right-side versions relevant to the *same committed snapshot*. The differential join then reconciles that row’s complete result for the snapshot, rather than treating each retraction or insert as an independent instruction to emit a null-extended row. If the row has no applicable match, its null-extended result belongs in the outer join once; if any applicable match exists, that null-extended result does not belong there.

That is the intended reasoning, not a claim that lineage alone prevents duplicates. The design must ensure that concurrent changes are evaluated against one snapshot and that their derived effects are reconciled before certified publication.
Why isn’t it enough to emit a null-extended row whenever a retraction removes what appears to be the last match?

Because “last” might describe an intermediate view of the key, not the committed snapshot being published. An insert included in that snapshot could supply another match. Two retractions could also independently see an apparent transition to no matches and each propose the same null-extended result.

The relevant question is whether the particular left-side row has any applicable match *after all changes belonging to that snapshot are accounted for*. Per-key lineage supplies the relevant contributors for that question; reconciliation determines the resulting output, rather than blindly adding together provisional emissions.
Are you saying concurrent operations must be processed in one fixed order?

Not as a requirement of this proposal. Internal work can be interleaved, but the published result must be the outer join of the base-table versions visible at the committed snapshot. The presence or absence of a null-extended result should follow that snapshot’s match state, not whichever operation happened to be processed first.

The proposal does not specify a scheduling or transaction-ordering protocol. It specifies per-key differential reconciliation under MVCC before publication.
Suppose a match is retracted and another is inserted for the same left-side row in the snapshot. What should happen to the null-extended row?

If the inserted match is applicable in that committed snapshot, the left-side row is not unmatched there, so no null-extended row should appear for it. The differential join still needs to remove the old matched result and add the new matched result as appropriate. What it must not do is publish a provisional null-extended result merely because it examined the retraction before the insertion.

That is a general illustration of the snapshot rule, not a statement about a particular transaction or data set.
And if the retraction leaves no applicable match after all those changes?

Then the outer join needs the applicable null-extended result for that left-side row, not one copy for every retraction that contributed to the no-match state. The per-key reconciliation should recognize the final transition to unmatched status for that row at the committed snapshot. Any aggregate over the join must also reflect the removal of matched contributions and the contribution, if any, of the null-extended result.
Does per-key mean there can only be one null-extended row for the entire join key?

No. Different left-side rows can share a join key, and each unmatched left-side row can require its own outer-join result. The distinction is between one applicable null-extended result *per unmatched left-side row occurrence* and accidental duplicates of that same result produced by concurrent processing. The proposal does not specify how row identity or multiplicity is represented in lineage.
What does lineage need to distinguish to make that distinction possible?

It needs to let the differential join relate the affected left-side rows to their applicable matching right-side inputs at the target MVCC snapshot. It also needs enough identity to avoid confusing two legitimate left-side row occurrences with two emissions of the same result. A per-key index can narrow the relevant search, but merely knowing the key is not sufficient if the calculation loses track of which left-side result it is reconciling.

That states information the approach would need; it does not prescribe an index entry format or a uniqueness mechanism.
If the lineage index shows two candidate matches, can the join simply count both?

Only if both are applicable matches in the committed snapshot and each represents a distinct contribution under the join’s semantics. MVCC lineage may contain information associated with different versions or transaction states. Treating every candidate entry as simultaneously visible could yield the wrong match state and therefore the wrong null-extended result.

The proposal relies on snapshot-aligned lineage and differential joining; it does not say how an index filters entries or represents multiplicity.
Could two workers each compute a zero-match result for the same row and both write it?

That is a concurrency case the design must prevent from becoming duplicate published output. Per-key lineage gives both workers a way to identify the relevant row and match state, but it does not by itself coordinate their writes. The reconciled view needs one effective null-extended contribution when that row is unmatched, regardless of how many provisional calculations occurred.

How the implementation combines, validates, or otherwise resolves those calculations is not specified. The observable requirement is the correct result at the committed snapshot.
Is a match count sufficient to solve the duplication problem?

A snapshot-correct count can tell the differential join whether matches remain, including the important zero-versus-nonzero transition. A count alone does not necessarily distinguish legitimate results for different left-side rows sharing a key, nor does it prevent two concurrent calculations from both materializing the same null-extended result. Counts, lineage, and the reconciliation of output contributions have related but distinct roles.

The proposal does not commit to a particular counting or output-deduplication implementation.
What if both an insert and a retraction occur, and the match count ends where it started?

An unchanged count does not necessarily mean an unchanged join result. One matched row may have disappeared and another may have appeared. The per-key differential join needs to account for those changed matched contributions even when the net number of matches is the same. For the null-extended result, what matters is whether the left-side row is unmatched in the snapshot being published; an unchanged positive count does not call for one.
Could a transient count of zero still affect an aggregate?

A provisional zero encountered while processing changes should not introduce a committed aggregate contribution from a null-extended row if the published snapshot has an applicable match. The aggregate must reflect the join result at that snapshot, not transient intermediate states. Conversely, if the snapshot truly leaves the row unmatched, the aggregate must account for the applicable null-extended result according to its expression.

The proposal does not name a specific aggregate, so it does not determine what numerical contribution that result makes.
How should retractions of left-side rows be handled in the same reasoning?

If a left-side row itself does not belong to the committed snapshot, it cannot contribute either matched joined results or a null-extended result there. Lineage-guided reconciliation therefore has to consider whether the left-side row is applicable as well as whether it has applicable matches. Otherwise, processing right-side changes alone could leave a null-extended output for a left-side row that is no longer present.

That is a general outer-join condition, not a new assertion about the workload or where left-side retractions occur.
Does certified snapshot publication do the deduplication?

Certification is the boundary for exposing the reconciled snapshot; it is not, by itself, an algorithm for finding duplicate null-extended rows. The per-key differential work must produce the right join and aggregate effects, and publication must wait for those required effects to be reconciled. Certifying an incorrectly duplicated result would not make it match full recomputation.
What if the computation for one affected key finishes while another affected key in the same transaction is still pending?

The completed key’s result cannot be treated as an independently published portion of the transaction if the committed snapshot requires the other key’s effects too. Per-key work localizes computation; certified publication governs the coherent snapshot visible to readers. This separation matters for both duplicate prevention at an individual key and atomic visibility across the transaction’s affected keys.
Does a partition failure change the rule for how many null-extended rows belong in a snapshot?

No. Failure and recovery can change when the required work becomes available, but not the outer-join result defined by a particular committed base-table snapshot. Recovery must not expose a provisional null-extended result from one participant while another participant has yet to supply an applicable match, or replay the same output contribution into the published view twice. The proposal does not define the recovery procedure that would enforce that behavior.
Is replaying the same lineage-derived change twice necessarily harmless?

Not automatically. If both applications add the same null-extended result or aggregate contribution, the maintained view could acquire a duplicate even though the base-table snapshot has only one applicable result for that left-side row. A complete implementation would need replay behavior that preserves the reconciled snapshot result under repetition. Per-key lineage helps identify which result is affected, but the proposal does not specify an idempotence method.
How can this remain incremental rather than scanning every partition to check for matches?

The intended role of partitioned lineage indexes is to locate the inputs relevant to the affected keys; per-key differential joins then evaluate the consequences for those keys. That is different from rescanning unaffected base-table partitions to rediscover the whole join. The approach still has to demonstrate that its lineage is complete and snapshot-correct, so it neither misses a match nor relies on an unaffected-partition rescan to find one.
Could an index lookup over the affected key be enough to tell whether a null-extended row is needed?

It can supply relevant evidence, but the answer also depends on whether the left-side row and the candidate matches are visible at the target snapshot and on whether concurrent changes for that key have been reconciled. An index lookup is not itself a committed-snapshot result. The proposal leaves open how the differential computation obtains and validates that complete picture.
What would be a direct correctness check for this duplicate-row concern?

For each committed snapshot being checked, compare the maintained outer join with full recomputation from the base tables at that same snapshot. In particular, for an applicable left-side row with no applicable matches, check that the maintained result has the null-extended contribution required by the join’s semantics—neither missing nor duplicated. For a row with a match, check that no spurious null-extended result appears. Check any dependent aggregate against that same recomputed snapshot as well.

That describes a way to evaluate the proposal, not a completed test or a reported outcome.
Does finding no duplicate null-extended rows prove all aggregate results are right?

No. The aggregate could still retain an old matched contribution, omit a new one, or otherwise disagree with recomputation. Avoiding duplicate null-extended rows is one necessary aspect of correct outer-join maintenance under concurrent changes; the resulting aggregate must also match the committed snapshot. Neither property should be inferred from the other alone.
Can you put the key idea into one concise rule?

For each applicable left-side row, derive the matched or null-extended output from its complete, snapshot-visible match state for the affected key; reconcile all concurrent inserts and retractions before certified publication, rather than emitting a null-extended row once per provisional zero-match event.

My hypothesis is that transaction-coalesced per-row match counts emit null-extension deltas only on zero-crossings, yielding zero recomputation mismatches across 100,000 snapshots. What exactly am I predicting?

You are predicting that, after changes are coalesced at the transaction level, each relevant row’s match count determines whether its null-extended outer-join result should appear or disappear. A null-extension delta is emitted only when that count crosses between zero and nonzero. The predicted outcome is zero differences from full recomputation across 100,000 snapshots.

That is a hypothesis about the proposed maintenance rule and its expected result, not a report that those snapshots have been tested.
Why specify a per-row count rather than just one count for a join key?

The null-extended result belongs to an applicable unmatched row, so the rule needs to distinguish that row’s match status. Several left-side rows could have the same join key without being the same output occurrence. A per-row count lets the hypothesis express the zero-crossing rule for each such row rather than treating all rows with a key as one null-extended result.

The hypothesis does not prescribe how row identity or count state is represented.
What does transaction-coalesced mean here?

It means considering the changes associated with a transaction together before deciding whether that transaction changes a row’s zero-versus-nonzero match status. A retraction might provisionally remove a match while an insertion in the same transaction supplies another. Emitting a null-extended result at the provisional zero, without considering both changes, could produce an output that does not belong to the transaction’s resulting snapshot.

Coalescing defines the scope of the decision; it does not say that all transactions are processed as one global batch.
Does coalescing mean ignoring individual retractions and inserts if their count changes cancel?

No. It means not treating an intermediate count as a reason to change *null-extension* status. Individual changes can still replace one matched join result with another, and their aggregate contributions may change even if the final match count is unchanged. The hypothesis restricts when null-extension deltas are emitted; it does not declare every other join or aggregate delta unnecessary.
What are the zero-crossings I should distinguish?

A transition from a positive match count to zero can make a null-extended result applicable for a left-side row that remains present. A transition from zero to a positive count can make that null-extended result cease to apply. A change between positive counts does not cross zero, and neither does a coalesced change whose count starts and ends at zero.

Those statements describe the null-extension rule. They do not mean the other changes have no effect on matched rows or aggregates.
When a count drops from one to zero, is the null-extension delta the only necessary view change?

No. The matched result associated with the retracted match also ceases to apply. The zero-crossing determines the additional null-extended result required by outer-join semantics. If an aggregate depends on the join, its maintained contributions must reflect the removal of the matched result and the introduction of any applicable null-extended result. The hypothesis singles out null-extension deltas rather than specifying all those other calculations.
And when it rises from zero to one?

The null-extended result ceases to apply, and the matched result becomes applicable. The null-extension delta is therefore in the opposite direction from the positive-to-zero case. Any dependent aggregate must follow the resulting join output at that snapshot. The actual contribution of either kind of row depends on the aggregate expression, which the hypothesis does not specify.
Suppose a transaction removes one match and adds another, leaving the per-row count at one. Should it emit a null-extension delta?

Not under the proposed zero-crossing rule: the coalesced count remains positive. The old matched result may need to be removed and the new matched result added, but a null-extended result would not belong to a snapshot in which that row still has an applicable match. This is a conceptual illustration, not a statement about a particular transaction in the 100,000 snapshots.
What if two matches are retracted in the same transaction and the count ends at zero?

The null-extension change should be based on the per-row transition from a positive count to zero, not emitted once for each retraction. That is how transaction coalescing and zero-crossing detection are intended to prevent duplicate null-extended output. Each removed matched result still needs to be accounted for separately where it contributed to the join or an aggregate.

The hypothesis does not specify the algorithm that combines the retractions or materializes the resulting row.
If the count stays at zero, why not emit the null-extended result again to be safe?

Because remaining at zero is not a transition into the unmatched state. For an applicable left-side row, its null-extended result already belongs to the before-and-after states under that match condition. Adding another copy merely because the transaction touched the key could create a duplicate rather than correct an omission.

A change to the left-side row itself might require separate handling; the count rule alone does not describe every way a row can enter or leave the outer join.

The row’s own presence must still be respected. A retracted left-side row should not contribute a null-extended result just because its match count is zero. What does LineageStore v2 contain?

LineageStore v2 atomically checkpoints per-key match counts together with applied transaction-row IDs. During recovery, it replays only the WAL suffixes for affected keys. Atomic checkpointing is meant to prevent that mismatch between the two kinds of state.

The artifact description does not specify the mechanism used to make the checkpoint atomic.

The two parts distinguish effects associated with different transactions and different rows. No. Checkpointed deduplicated replay is a maintenance and recovery approach; full recomputation remains a way to check whether a committed view has the right result.
