So what is the tightest wording if I want the choice and its stated reasons, without a broader guarantee?
“Adopt LineageStore v2: its checkpointed, deduplicated replay eliminates the four duplicate-delta mismatches and twelve unaffected-partition rescans.”
I propose maintaining MVCC per-group SUM/COUNT and counted MIN/MAX trees from LineageStore v2 deltas, then publishing transaction-wide versions via ApplyCert v1. How do the pieces fit together?

LineageStore v2 deltas provide the changes to be reflected in the maintained view. For each affected group, MVCC per-group state would track SUM and COUNT, while counted MIN/MAX trees would track the values and their multiplicities needed to maintain extrema through insertions and retractions. ApplyCert v1 would govern when the resulting transaction-wide versions can be published as a committed snapshot.

The proposal separates computing aggregate changes from making a coherent version visible. It does not yet establish that every resulting aggregate matches full recomputation.
What does MVCC add to per-group aggregate state?

It lets the aggregate state be interpreted at a particular committed snapshot. Work for one transaction can be in progress while readers still need the SUM, COUNT, MIN, and MAX values belonging to an earlier visible snapshot. A group value assembled from changes belonging to different snapshot states would not meet the snapshot-consistency requirement.

The proposal does not specify how versions are stored, retained, or selected by a reader.
Are SUM and COUNT being maintained as one global total?

No. The proposal says *per-group* SUM/COUNT. A delta affecting one group should change the appropriate version of that group’s state; it does not, by itself, imply a change to every other group. The proposal does not define the grouping expressions or where groups are placed across shards.
Why name SUM and COUNT together?

Both can be maintained by accounting for the contributions added to and removed from a group. For an applicable value, an insertion can add its contribution to SUM and COUNT, and a retraction can remove the contribution it previously made. Their exact handling still depends on the query’s aggregate semantics, including which input values qualify.

Naming them together does not mean that COUNT is necessarily the number of base-table rows rather than the number of qualifying contributions to a particular aggregate expression.
Does a retraction always subtract the row’s raw base-table value from SUM?

Not automatically. The contribution to retract must be the contribution the relevant joined result made to that group at the snapshot where it applied. An outer join can change which joined result exists when a match disappears, so a retraction may remove a matched contribution and make a different null-extended result applicable. The proposal does not define the SUM expression or its treatment of null values; the maintained result must follow the expression’s semantics.
What makes MIN and MAX harder to maintain under retractions?

Removing one contribution to SUM or COUNT suggests a corresponding signed change. Removing the current minimum or maximum is different: the resulting extremum depends on what other values remain in the group. A counted MIN/MAX tree is proposed to retain that information, including how many applicable contributions of a value are present, so a retraction can be evaluated against the remaining values.

The proposal does not specify a tree implementation or the rules for a group with no qualifying values.
Why is the tree counted instead of just storing the smallest and largest values?

If multiple contributions have the same minimum, retracting one does not necessarily change MIN. A count for that value distinguishes removal of one occurrence from removal of the last occurrence. If the last occurrence disappears, the remaining values determine the next minimum. The same reasoning applies to MAX.

This is a general illustration of the counted-tree role, not a statement about a particular group or data set.
If a non-extreme value is retracted, does it matter to the tree?

Yes. Its multiplicity changes even if the current MIN and MAX stay the same. It could matter to a later snapshot if more extreme values are subsequently retracted. Maintaining the tree’s counted contents and publishing a change to the visible extremum are distinct questions.
Suppose a transaction retracts one minimum value and inserts another value. Should the tree expose its intermediate minimum?

Not as a committed result merely because one delta was processed first. The group’s version for the transaction should reflect the applicable changes together at the committed snapshot. An internal intermediate extremum could differ from the final extremum without being a value that readers should observe as a transaction-wide published version.

The proposal does not dictate the order in which the internal deltas are processed.
What is the role of the LineageStore v2 deltas in determining which group changes?

They are the proposed inputs to aggregate maintenance. A change to the maintained join result can remove a contribution from a group, add one, or do both where the applicable result changes. The aggregate state has to use the deltas corresponding to the snapshot-consistent view change, rather than treating an unrelated base-table update as an automatic change to every group.

The proposal does not define the delta format, grouping expressions, or a method for locating every affected group.
How do null-extended outer-join rows enter the aggregate calculation?

They enter according to the aggregate expressions applied to the join output. If an outer-join row changes from matched to null-extended, contributions from the former joined result may need removal, and contributions from the applicable null-extended result must be handled as the expressions require. COUNT, SUM, MIN, and MAX need not treat a null-extended row identically.

The proposal does not give the expressions or their null-handling rules, so no universal numerical adjustment can be assigned to that transition.
Could the per-group COUNT disagree with the match count used by an outer join without either being a corrupted counter?

Yes. They count different things. An outer-join match count concerns how many applicable matches a row has; a group’s aggregate COUNT concerns qualifying contributions to the COUNT expression. They may legitimately have different values. They must nevertheless be derived from mutually consistent transaction and snapshot states when the view is published.
What if a joined result moves from one group to another?

Conceptually, the old group must cease to include its former contribution, and the new group must receive the applicable contribution. Any resulting SUM/COUNT changes and MIN/MAX multiplicity changes need to be reflected in the versions published for that transaction. The proposal does not state which changes can cause a group move or specify a particular grouping expression.
Does transaction-wide publication mean every group in the whole system needs a new version for each transaction?

Not necessarily. “Transaction-wide” concerns the visibility of that transaction’s required effects together, not an instruction to rewrite unaffected groups. The proposal maintains per-group state from deltas and publishes transaction-wide versions through ApplyCert v1. It leaves open the physical version representation and how unaffected groups remain visible at a snapshot.
If a transaction affects SUM on one shard and MIN on another, can the first shard publish its new aggregate independently?

Not as a partial committed version of the transaction. The proposed publication boundary is transaction-wide: a reader of a committed snapshot should see the required aggregate effects together with the corresponding join and base-table state. One shard completing its SUM update does not establish that the MIN effect or other required participant work is ready to publish.

ApplyCert v1 provides a gate for checking the required current-generation participants; the proposal does not specify where any particular aggregate is stored.
What does ApplyCert v1 certify in this arrangement?

Its role is to provide transaction-digest-bound, generation-fenced shard application evidence and a publication gate that verifies all required current-generation participants. For this proposal, that gate would control visibility of the transaction-wide versions after their required effects are applied. A valid certificate is not a mathematical proof that a computed SUM or MIN is correct; computation and publication remain separate obligations.
Could an apply certificate be accepted before a counted tree has incorporated a required retraction?

A certificate used to publish that transaction’s aggregate version must not be taken as evidence of complete application if a required tree change remains unapplied. Otherwise, the publication boundary could expose a snapshot whose MIN or MAX does not reflect its retraction. The proposal does not define the certificate’s exact coverage or issuance procedure, so ensuring it represents all required aggregate work is a design obligation, not an established implementation detail.
What if the certificate has the right transaction digest but comes from a superseded shard generation?

ApplyCert v1’s generation fence means it must not satisfy the current-generation participant check merely because the digest matches. Transaction identity and generation validity are separate conditions. The proposal uses that publication gate for transaction-wide versions; it does not specify how a shard obtains applicable evidence after a generation change.
How should crash recovery treat aggregate state that has been calculated but not published?

It must preserve the distinction between internal recovered work and a committed visible version. The eventual published aggregate state has to reflect the transaction’s required deltas exactly as the relevant snapshot requires, without omitting a contribution or incorporating it twice. ApplyCert v1 governs publication evidence, while LineageStore v2 deltas supply the changes this proposal would aggregate.

The proposal does not specify how aggregate versions or counted trees are persisted or replayed after a crash.
Does LineageStore v2’s applied transaction-row ID tell us whether an aggregate delta has already been applied?

It identifies effects accounted for in LineageStore v2’s checkpointed lineage state. The proposal does not say that the same record automatically proves a per-group SUM/COUNT update or counted MIN/MAX-tree update has been applied. If recovery can repeat input deltas, aggregate application must still avoid repeated effective contributions. The coordination between lineage recovery state and aggregate recovery state is not specified here.
If a repeated retraction decreases a counted minimum’s multiplicity twice, could publication still be atomic?

It could be published as one coherent transaction version yet have the wrong MIN result. Atomic visibility prevents exposing part of a transaction; it does not correct a duplicated calculation. The counted tree needs the right effective multiplicities, and the published value must match full recomputation at that committed snapshot.
What happens when the last qualifying value in a group is removed?

The tree would no longer have that value as an available minimum or maximum. What result the query should expose for an empty set of qualifying values depends on the aggregate and grouping semantics, which are not specified. The proposal needs to preserve those semantics; it should not invent a replacement extremum or assume that the group necessarily disappears.
Can an unchanged SUM and COUNT tell us that MIN and MAX are also unchanged?

No. Changes can offset in SUM and COUNT while altering the set or multiplicity of values available to MIN and MAX. That is one reason the proposal maintains counted MIN/MAX trees alongside per-group SUM/COUNT rather than deriving extrema from those two totals alone.
Could MIN and MAX remain unchanged while a transaction still requires a tree update?

Yes. Adding or removing a value that is not the visible extremum can change its count in the tree without changing the current MIN or MAX. Keeping the counted state accurate matters for later retractions. The absence of an immediate extremum change does not mean the transaction had no effect on the maintained tree.
Do the proposed trees require scanning every base-table partition if the current minimum is removed?

Their intended role is to retain the group’s counted candidate values so the next applicable extremum can be determined from maintained state, rather than discovered by rescanning unaffected base-table partitions. The proposal alone does not demonstrate that the tree has complete, recoverable information in every case. Avoidance of unaffected-partition rescans remains a constraint to verify, including during recovery.
Does maintaining versions require globally pausing writers before every publication?

No global pause is specified. MVCC separates work on newer state from what an existing committed snapshot exposes, and the proposed transaction-wide publication waits for the required applied effects rather than saying that all writers must stop. Whether an implementation actually maintains writer progress without a global pause is an operational question the proposal does not measure.
How would you evaluate the proposal against the original correctness requirement?

At every committed snapshot across 100,000 transactions, including crash recovery, compare the maintained outer joins and per-group SUM, COUNT, MIN, and MAX with full recomputation from base tables at that same snapshot. Check that a transaction affecting multiple tables or groups does not expose a mixture of versions, and that retractions change both null-extended join results and aggregate contributions as required.

That describes the correctness target and a comparison, not a completed experiment or an observed result for this proposal.
Would matching the aggregates at the final snapshot suffice?

No. An intermediate committed snapshot could expose an incorrect extremum after a retraction or a partial multi-group transaction and later become correct. The requirement is equality at *every* committed snapshot in the 100,000-transaction scope, including crash recovery, not merely at its endpoint.
If all aggregate comparisons match, does that also establish there were no rescans of unaffected base-table partitions?

No. Correct aggregate values and maintenance scan behavior are separate properties. Counted trees and lineage deltas are proposed ways to maintain affected state incrementally, but a comparison with full recomputation does not reveal what the maintenance path scanned. Avoiding rescans of unaffected base-table partitions must be checked as an operational condition in its own right.
Is full recomputation being proposed as the way to update these trees?

No. The proposal says to maintain MVCC per-group SUM/COUNT and counted MIN/MAX trees *from LineageStore v2 deltas*. Full recomputation is the reference for determining whether the maintained results at a snapshot are correct; it is not the proposed update method.
Can you state the whole proposal succinctly, preserving the maintenance and publication order?

“Maintain MVCC per-group SUM/COUNT and counted MIN/MAX trees from LineageStore v2 deltas, then publish the transaction-wide versions through ApplyCert v1.” The intended ordering is to incorporate the required join-derived and aggregate changes before exposing their coherent committed-snapshot version.
How can MIN/MAX replace retracted extrema without scanning unaffected partitions or exposing partially updated aggregate groups?

The proposed counted MIN/MAX tree keeps the candidate values and their multiplicities in maintained per-group state. When an extremal contribution is retracted, its count changes: if another occurrence remains, the extremum need not change; if the last occurrence is removed, the tree can identify the next applicable value from its maintained state rather than scanning unaffected base-table partitions.

That calculation is separate from visibility. The resulting group changes would be maintained as MVCC versions from the relevant LineageStore v2 deltas, then exposed through a transaction-wide ApplyCert v1 publication boundary only when the required participant effects are ready. This explains the intended approach, not a demonstrated correctness or scan result.
Why is keeping just the current minimum and maximum insufficient?

If the last occurrence of the current minimum disappears, those two values alone do not identify the next minimum. The counted tree is proposed to retain other applicable values in the group, so replacing an extremum draws on already maintained group state. Multiplicities matter too: retracting one of several equal minima should not promote a different value prematurely.
If one minimum is removed but another equal minimum remains, is there a replacement to publish?

The visible MIN remains the same. The count of that value in the group’s maintained state still needs to decrease, because a later retraction could remove its last remaining occurrence. A change to the counted state and a change to the exposed extremum are therefore different things.
What if the retracted value is not currently MIN or MAX?

Its multiplicity still needs updating if it contributed to the group. The currently visible extrema may remain unchanged, but the value may become relevant to a later replacement. Ignoring non-extremal retractions would make the maintained candidates unreliable when an extremum eventually disappears.
Where does the tree get the candidate values without reading other base-table partitions during a retraction?

The proposal is to maintain its counted group contents incrementally from LineageStore v2 deltas as contributions arrive and leave. When an extremum is retracted, the replacement is sought among those maintained candidates rather than reconstructed by scanning unaffected base-table partitions. That depends on the tree containing the complete applicable group contributions at the snapshot in question; merely naming a tree does not establish that completeness or describe its storage layout.
Does “unaffected partition” mean an unaffected group?

No. A base-table partition and an aggregate group are different concepts. The requirement rules out rescanning base-table partitions unaffected by the change. Identifying and updating the aggregate groups actually affected by a LineageStore v2 delta remains necessary, regardless of how groups and base-table partitions are placed. No particular placement is specified.
Could a group span several base-table partitions?

The proposal does not constrain a group to one partition. If a group’s contributions are distributed, the maintained counted state still needs to represent its applicable values, and publication must account for all required participant effects. It would not be sound to assume the next extremum can be found by looking only at the partition that held the retracted value unless the maintained group state supports that conclusion.
If the current minimum disappears, should the tree report the next value immediately?

It may calculate a prospective new MIN while processing the transaction, but that internal calculation need not become a committed result immediately. Other deltas in the same transaction might alter that group too. The published MVCC group version should reflect the combined effects applicable at the committed snapshot, not an intermediate state seen while processing one retraction.
Suppose the same transaction removes an old minimum and inserts another value. Does the order of internal updates determine what readers see?

It should not. The visible group result must agree with the transaction’s committed-snapshot input, however the internal work is ordered. The counted state has to incorporate both relevant changes before that transaction-wide version becomes visible. An intermediate minimum after removal but before insertion is not automatically a separate committed snapshot.
How would concurrent transactions touching the same group affect that rule?

Each published MVCC version needs to correspond to a coherent committed snapshot. The counted tree cannot combine a retraction visible in one snapshot with an insertion that belongs only to another and present the mixture as a committed MIN or MAX. The proposal does not supply a concurrency-control algorithm for simultaneous group updates; snapshot-aligned results and coherent publication are the requirements it would have to uphold.
What does it mean not to expose a partially updated aggregate group?

A reader should not see, for a committed snapshot, a group whose MIN reflects a retraction while its MAX, SUM, COUNT, or other required changes still reflect a different transaction state. Nor should a multi-group or multi-table transaction expose the new version of only one affected group as though its other required effects were already present. Internal progress may differ; the committed view must not present that progress as a partially applied transaction.
Does each affected group have to change all four aggregate values?

No. A retraction can change counted state without changing a visible extremum, and different aggregate expressions may respond differently. The constraint is that whatever SUM, COUNT, MIN, and MAX values are applicable for a group at a snapshot must be presented consistently. Transaction-wide visibility does not mean inventing a numerical change to every aggregate whenever a group is touched.
How does MVCC help keep an intermediate tree update from leaking to readers?

MVCC gives the proposal separate versioned states for the committed snapshots being read and the effects being prepared for a newer snapshot. A reader can use the published version while changes to an affected group are still being reconciled. That separation only works if version selection and publication are consistent; MVCC as a label alone does not prevent a partially updated value from being exposed.
What does ApplyCert v1 contribute beyond versioning the group?

Versioning allows the group state for different snapshots to be distinguished. ApplyCert v1 supplies the proposed transaction-wide publication gate, using transaction-digest-bound, generation-fenced shard certificates and checking the required current-generation participants. The gate is intended to keep a group’s updated version and the transaction’s other required effects behind one visibility boundary. It does not calculate the replacement extremum or prove that the counted tree contains the right values.
Could one shard publish a new MIN once its tree is ready, while another shard is still applying the same transaction’s aggregate delta?

Not as a committed transaction-wide snapshot. Readiness of one shard’s tree is an internal milestone; it cannot stand in for the other required participant’s applied work. The proposal calls for transaction-wide versions through ApplyCert v1 so readers do not encounter only the new MIN while another required effect of that transaction remains pending.
Does an apply certificate guarantee that the next minimum chosen by the tree is correct?

No. It is application evidence bound to a transaction and shard generation, not a mathematical check of the tree’s replacement value. The tree and its updates must be correct independently. Comparing the maintained view with full recomputation at the same committed snapshot would check the resulting MIN and MAX values.
How does an outer-join retraction reach a MIN/MAX group?

The aggregate is over the applicable join results. Retracting a match may remove a matched contribution and, if it removes the last match for an applicable left-side row, make a null-extended result applicable. LineageStore v2 deltas are proposed as the input changes from which the per-group state is maintained. The aggregate expression determines whether and how either joined result contributes a value to MIN or MAX; that expression is not specified.
Would the null-extended result always become the new minimum if the last match disappears?

No. The result’s contribution depends on the MIN expression and its null semantics. A null-extended row is not a license to assume a particular numerical value or a particular new minimum. The proposal has to use the aggregate’s actual qualifying contributions and match full recomputation for the committed snapshot.
What if a retraction removes the last qualifying value in a group?

Then the counted tree has no remaining qualifying value from which to choose a replacement. The exposed result must follow the query’s semantics for that group and aggregate in that situation. Those semantics are not specified here, so the answer should not invent a sentinel value or assume that the group necessarily disappears.
Would a correct MIN/MAX result also prove SUM and COUNT were correctly updated?

No. MIN/MAX can remain unchanged while a retraction changes SUM or COUNT, and SUM/COUNT can remain unchanged while the distribution of values in the counted tree changes. The maintained values must each reflect the applicable deltas at the same snapshot. Agreement of one aggregate is not proof of the others.
Could maintaining the tree cause a scan of an unaffected partition even if the result is correct?

That is an operational possibility a design must rule out, not something established by value correctness. The intended method finds the replacement from maintained counted state instead of rescanning unaffected base-table partitions. A recomputation comparison checks the answer, while a separate observation of maintenance and recovery reads would be needed to show that those partitions were not rescanned.
How should recovery handle an extremal retraction whose aggregate changes have not all been restored?

It must not publish an MVCC snapshot that relies on the new extremum while required group or transaction effects remain unavailable. Recovery would need to restore the applicable counted state and other aggregate contributions before their transaction-wide version becomes visible. ApplyCert v1 is the proposed publication boundary; the proposal does not specify how aggregate-tree state is checkpointed or replayed after a failure.
Would recomputing MIN/MAX after every shard crash solve the correctness question?

It could serve as a correctness reference, but using broad base-table recomputation as the recovery path would conflict with the constraint against rescanning unaffected base-table partitions if it included them. The proposed maintenance method is to use deltas and counted trees; full recomputation is the benchmark for evaluating their snapshot results, not the prescribed method for updating them.
What exact comparison would check the replacement extremum?

For a committed snapshot in which an extremal contribution was retracted, compare the maintained group’s MIN and MAX with those obtained by fully recomputing that group’s aggregates from the base-table state of the same snapshot, through the applicable outer join. Check SUM and COUNT there as well if the transaction affects them. This describes a correctness check, not a reported experiment or result.
And how would you check the absence of partial aggregate visibility?

Examine committed reads at the publication boundary: all required group versions and other transaction effects visible in a snapshot should correspond to that one snapshot, not a mixture of before-and-after states. An internal tree update does not count as partial visibility unless it leaks into a committed read. Comparing a published result with recomputation is another way to detect an inconsistent output, but the publication condition itself must still cover all required participants.
Can you summarize the answer to my original question in one rule?

Maintain complete, counted per-group candidate values from the relevant deltas so a retracted last extremum can be replaced from maintained state, not by rescanning unaffected base-table partitions; make the resulting MVCC aggregate versions visible only with the transaction’s other required effects through the ApplyCert v1 publication boundary.

Here is the plan for MIN/MAX: update per-group counted B-trees with coalesced signed deltas, stage replacement extrema under MVCC, and publish after ApplyCert validation. Can you walk through the ordering?

First, coalesce the relevant changes so each affected group’s counted B-tree receives the appropriate additions and retractions. Use the resulting counted state to determine any replacement MIN or MAX. Stage those replacement extrema as MVCC state rather than exposing them immediately. Publish the transaction’s resulting versions only after ApplyCert validation.

That is the planned order, not a claim that the updates or validation have already been implemented or tested.
What does a counted B-tree need to retain for a group?

Conceptually, it retains qualifying candidate values and their multiplicities. If one occurrence of the current minimum is retracted, a remaining occurrence can keep MIN unchanged. If the last occurrence is retracted, the maintained candidates can identify the next applicable extremum without seeking it by rescanning unaffected base-table partitions.

The plan does not specify the B-tree layout, the value representation, or how a particular aggregate expression determines qualifying contributions.
Why use a separate tree for each group?

MIN and MAX are defined over the contributions to a particular group. Per-group counted state lets a change be applied to the groups it affects and lets the replacement extremum be determined from that group’s remaining candidates. It does not mean that every group must change for every transaction, and the plan does not specify where the trees are stored.
What does “signed” mean for a B-tree update?

A positive delta represents an added qualifying contribution, while a negative delta represents a contribution being removed. The tree’s count for the relevant value changes accordingly. This is about contribution multiplicity, not about whether the value itself is a positive or negative number. The plan does not provide an encoding for signed deltas or a particular aggregate expression.
Why coalesce those deltas before updating the tree?

Coalescing lets the tree update reflect the combined relevant changes rather than treating every provisional processing step as a committed group state. For example, a retraction and insertion could affect the same group within one transaction; an intermediate extremum encountered after only the retraction need not be the extremum of the resulting committed snapshot. The plan does not specify a coalescing algorithm or claim that all transactions are processed in one global batch.
If one occurrence of a minimum is retracted but others remain, what is staged?

The counted state must reflect the reduced multiplicity, but the visible minimum need not change. If a staged group version is required for the transaction, its MIN should still be the same applicable value. The important distinction is that an unchanged extremum does not make the retraction irrelevant to the counted B-tree.
What if the retraction removes the final occurrence of the minimum?

The tree’s remaining qualifying values determine the replacement minimum, if one exists. That replacement belongs in the staged MVCC group state for the relevant transaction, not in an independently published intermediate result. The same principle applies to retracting the last occurrence of a maximum. If no qualifying value remains, the visible result must follow the query’s aggregate semantics, which the plan does not specify.
Does finding a replacement require searching every base-table partition that contributes to the group?

The intended approach is to find it in the maintained counted B-tree, rather than rescan unaffected base-table partitions. That requires the tree to represent the applicable candidate contributions correctly. Naming the tree does not by itself prove that it is complete or that a particular implementation performs no unaffected-partition rescans.
If a non-extreme value is retracted, can I skip the tree update?

No. Its count still matters to the group’s maintained candidate set, even if MIN and MAX do not change immediately. A later retraction of an extremum may make that value relevant as a replacement. The plan updates counted B-trees with the applicable signed deltas, rather than updating them only when the visible extremum changes.
Can a signed delta remove a value that the current group version does not contain?

The planned update has to correspond to an actual contribution applicable to the version being maintained. A removal that is not supported by the relevant group state would risk an incorrect count and extremum. The plan does not specify validation or error handling for such a delta, so it should not be treated as defining a recovery procedure for that case.
How do null-extended outer-join rows affect the B-tree?

A transition between matched and null-extended join results can change the contributions to an aggregate group. Coalesced signed deltas would remove contributions from results that cease to apply and add any qualifying contributions from results that become applicable. Whether a null-extended row contributes to a particular MIN or MAX expression depends on that expression’s semantics; it cannot be assigned a numerical value merely because it is null-extended.
Would coalescing the deltas guarantee that the outer join itself is correct?

No. Coalescing governs how changes presented to an aggregate group are combined. The underlying joined results—including whether a null-extended row is applicable—must still be correct for the committed snapshot. A perfectly updated B-tree using an incorrect join delta could produce an aggregate that disagrees with full recomputation.
Why stage the replacement extremum under MVCC instead of changing the value readers see immediately?

Staging separates internal aggregate work from committed-snapshot visibility. A replacement determined while the transaction is being processed may need to become visible along with other group, join, and table effects. MVCC lets the planned group version be distinguished from the version readers currently see; ApplyCert validation then precedes publication of the transaction’s resulting state.

The plan does not define how MVCC versions are stored or selected.
If the tree has been updated but ApplyCert validation is still pending, which MIN should a committed reader see?

The reader should not see the staged replacement solely because the tree update finished. The committed version exposed to that reader must remain consistent with its published snapshot. The planned ordering is tree update, MVCC staging, and then publication after validation—not independent visibility as each group finishes.
Could one group have its replacement staged while another affected group is still being updated?

Yes, internal progress can differ. Staging the first group does not make the multi-group transaction partly visible. Publication must wait for the required transaction effects and ApplyCert validation so a committed reader does not see one group’s new extremum alongside another required group’s old state.
What does ApplyCert validate for this publication step?

ApplyCert v1 provides transaction-digest-bound, generation-fenced shard certificates and a publication gate verifying the required current-generation participants. In this plan, publication follows that validation so a participant’s staged aggregate version is not exposed independently of the other required transaction effects. A certificate is application evidence; it does not, on its own, prove that the selected MIN or MAX is mathematically correct.
If the certificate identifies the right transaction, can publication proceed even if an affected B-tree has not received its delta?

Not if the certificate is being used to attest that the transaction’s required effects have been applied. A missing B-tree update would leave a required aggregate effect absent from the published snapshot. The plan does not define exactly how certificate issuance covers B-tree application, so that relationship must be made sound rather than assumed from matching the transaction digest alone.
And if a shard’s certificate comes from a superseded generation?

ApplyCert’s generation fence means such a certificate must not be counted as valid current-generation evidence for publication. The staged aggregate state and publication evidence must refer to the transaction and the relevant participant context. This plan does not specify how an applicable certificate is obtained after a generation change.
Does ApplyCert validation cause the B-tree to calculate the replacement extremum?

No. The counted B-tree update and MVCC staging produce the proposed group result. ApplyCert validation governs whether the necessary applied effects can support transaction-wide publication. Separating those roles is important: correct publication of an incorrect replacement would still yield the wrong aggregate.
What if SUM and COUNT also change in the same group?

Their applicable changes need to be reflected in the group version published with the staged MIN or MAX. The counted B-tree specifically addresses extrema and multiplicities; it does not replace the proposed maintenance of per-group SUM and COUNT. A committed reader should see values corresponding to the same transaction and snapshot, not a staged MIN with older SUM or COUNT.
Does this plan require a new B-tree version for every group on every transaction?

It says to update per-group counted B-trees with coalesced signed deltas and stage replacement extrema under MVCC. It does not require rewriting unaffected groups or specify the physical granularity of MVCC versions. Transaction-wide publication concerns the required affected effects becoming visible coherently, not an obligation to change every group.
Could an update leave SUM and COUNT unchanged while still changing MIN?

Conceptually, yes: totals alone do not describe the distribution of candidate values in a group. A combination of removals and additions may leave certain totals unchanged while altering an extremum. That is why the proposed counted B-tree has a distinct role alongside SUM and COUNT. Whether a particular change has that effect depends on its actual contributions.
How should concurrent transactions affecting the same group be interpreted?

The staged versions and counted updates must ultimately correspond to their respective committed snapshots. One published group value cannot combine a retraction from one snapshot with an insertion not yet visible there. The plan names coalesced signed deltas, MVCC staging, and ApplyCert publication, but does not specify the concurrency-control method for resolving simultaneous work on a group.
Does coalescing mean that a retraction can be canceled without recording its effect on the counted tree?

It does not authorize losing a legitimate change. Coalescing determines the combined contribution change for the version being maintained. If a value is retracted and an equivalent qualifying contribution is added, the effective multiplicity for that value may be unchanged, while other joined results or group state could still change. The implementation must derive the correct net tree state rather than assume that all paired events are interchangeable.
How would crash recovery affect a staged replacement minimum?

Recovery must distinguish a replacement calculated internally from one that belongs to a published committed snapshot. The relevant deltas, counted state, and MVCC version need to support whichever snapshot is eventually exposed, with publication still following ApplyCert validation. This plan does not specify how B-tree state or staged extrema are persisted and replayed through a crash.

I propose gating each transaction’s snapshot on generation-fenced certificates covering both lineage replay and all affected aggregate-group updates. How should that publication rule work conceptually?

Treat publication as a transaction-level boundary. Not necessarily. The proposal requires generation-fenced certificates that, taken as the publication evidence, cover both lineage replay and all affected aggregate-group updates. What matters is that the gate cannot infer aggregate completion from evidence that attests only to lineage replay, or vice versa.

If either required change remains outside the certified applied state, the transaction’s aggregate result is not ready for publication under this proposal.

The proposal does not specify grouping expressions or where those groups are stored.

Its requirement is complete coverage of the work the transaction actually requires.

The proposal does not specify the aggregate expression or the numerical effect of that null-extended result.

It prevents evidence from a superseded generation from being counted as if it were valid for the generation governing publication. That applies to evidence covering lineage replay and to evidence covering affected aggregate-group updates. During a leadership change, a certificate’s continued existence alone should not make it suitable for a newer snapshot gate.

The proposal does not define how generations are numbered, checked, or renewed.

Each required portion of the transaction’s work must have appropriate generation-fenced coverage before the snapshot is exposed.

Not necessarily. Establishing valid evidence for a new generation is different from applying an already incorporated delta a second time. The proposal does not specify how work is checked or recertified after a generation change; it requires that whatever evidence authorizes publication be valid for the relevant generation and cover the required applied effects.

They could change which generation-fenced evidence is applicable. How does the gate know the source and destination groups are the complete affected set?

If a transaction moves more than one contribution, is a single source and destination certificate pair automatically enough?

Should an unaffected group issue a certificate just to let this move publish?

What if the destination insertion is applied, but a failover makes the source deletion’s earlier certificate inapplicable?

A certificate can accurately identify the source-group deletion as required work yet attest to it prematurely if that work remains staged rather than durably applied. GroupMove100K reports one mismatch under precisely that distinction.
Is this evidence of an expired generation fence?

No. The certificate is explicitly described as *current-generation*. The finding does not identify an expired or superseded generation. It shows why passing a generation check is not equivalent to establishing durable application of the affected aggregate update.
Would calling it a digest mismatch be accurate?

No. “Digest-complete” is part of the finding. The reported mismatch is between the maintained aggregate result and recomputation, not a stated mismatch between transaction digests. Keep those two uses of “mismatch” separate.
What did recomputation reveal that inspecting the certificate alone might miss?

The GroupMove100K comparison found one disagreement in the maintained results. A certificate’s current generation and complete digest did not establish that its attested source-group deletion had been durably applied. Recomputing from the corresponding committed snapshot provides a reference for the resulting aggregate value, while the certificate conditions concern the evidence used around publication.

The finding does not give the individual aggregate values in that comparison.
Can I infer which of SUM, COUNT, MIN, or MAX mismatched?

No. The finding reports one mismatch and identifies the prematurely attested source-group deletion, but does not name the aggregate function or provide a value. A source-group contribution can matter to different aggregate expressions; assigning this mismatch to one of them would add an unsupported detail.
Does this tell us anything specific about the destination group’s insertion?

It does not characterize the destination-group insertion. The concrete operation named in this finding is the *source-group deletion*. We should not infer that the destination insertion was missing, duplicated, durably applied, or unaffected merely from the one reported mismatch.
Was the source-group deletion necessarily lost during a crash?

No such loss is stated. The finding says the certificate attested while the deletion was staged and *before durable application*. It does not say the deletion was permanently lost, identify a crash at that moment, or state whether application completed later. Premature attestation is the reported timing problem.
Could a later durable application erase the mismatch?

It would not undo a mismatch already observed in the comparison. The finding does not say whether the deletion was later durably applied or what later snapshots contained. Report the mismatch and the premature attestation without adding an eventual correction or persistence claim.
Is this evidence that a group-version fence was absent or stale?

The finding does not report a missing or stale group-version fence. It identifies a current-generation, digest-complete certificate attesting a staged source-group deletion before durable application. A group-version fence and an application attestation address different conditions, so the observed premature attestation should not be relabeled as a fence failure.
Can I say the certificate proved the deletion had been applied but it had not been persisted?

That wording would assume more than the finding gives. It says the deletion was *staged* and had not been *durably applied* when the certificate attested it. It does not specify whether an in-memory aggregate change had occurred, what persistence step was outstanding, or the exact meaning of durable application in the implementation. The safe formulation retains “staged” and “before durable application.”
What is the publication distinction this observation makes visible?

Being able to present a current-generation, digest-complete certificate is not sufficient if it attests to required aggregate work before that work is durably applied. For a transaction’s published aggregate to represent its committed snapshot, evidence covering a source-group deletion must reflect completed application rather than an intention or staged operation. That is the correctness distinction illustrated by the one mismatch; the finding does not specify a new publication mechanism.
Does a source-group deletion always change the visible minimum or maximum?

No. Removing a contribution can leave an extremum unchanged if another qualifying occurrence remains, while still changing the group’s counted state. The finding does not say which aggregate changed in this case. The essential observation is that the attestation preceded durable application of a required source-group deletion and GroupMove100K found one mismatch.
Can I call this a partial snapshot?

The reported measurement is *one mismatch*, not a separately counted partial snapshot. Prematurely attesting an aggregate update raises a snapshot-consistency concern, but the finding does not provide a partial-snapshot or partial-read count. Describe the observed recomputation mismatch rather than substituting another measurement.
Does the test name tell us how many snapshots were compared in this run?

No comparison count is supplied in this finding. GroupMove100K identifies the test, but the node reports only one mismatch and the condition of the source-group certificate. Do not derive a number of compared snapshots, transactions, or certificates from the test name.
Would it be fair to say the certificate checked readiness instead of durable application?

You can say it *attested a staged deletion before durable application*. Calling that a particular implemented “readiness check” would add detail the finding does not give. The supported distinction is between the observed attestation and the durable-application condition it preceded.
Does the finding show that all current-generation, digest-complete certificates are unreliable?

No. It identifies one mismatch in which a certificate with those properties attested too early. That shows those properties alone did not establish durable application in the reported case. It does not give a total certificate count or characterize every other certificate in GroupMove100K or elsewhere.
Can we infer whether writers were paused or unaffected partitions were rescanned?

No. The finding concerns one recomputation mismatch and premature attestation of a staged source-group deletion. It gives no writer-progress measurement, pause observation, or unaffected-partition scan count. Those operational questions remain outside this reported result.
What is the most compact interpretation that preserves the exact failure boundary without proposing an untested fix?

GroupMove100K found one mismatch because a current-generation, digest-complete certificate attested a source-group deletion while it was staged, before durable application. The result distinguishes valid-looking certificate identity and generation from completed aggregate application; it does not prescribe how to change certification.

I’m deciding to retain group-complete certificates, but issue them only after durable aggregate application and atomic fence checkpoints. Earlier passes missed both defects. How should I state that decision?

“Retain group-complete certificates, but issue them only after the required aggregate updates are durably applied and their group-version fences are atomically checkpointed; earlier passes missed both defects.” This preserves the choice, the two issuance prerequisites, and the stated limitation of the earlier passes. It does not claim that the strengthened rule has already been implemented or tested.
What does retaining group-complete certificates preserve?

It preserves the requirement that publication evidence cover every aggregate group affected by a transaction. For a cross-shard group move, that includes the required source-group removal and destination-group addition. The decision strengthens *when* such certificates may be issued; it does not abandon their all-affected-groups coverage.
Why isn’t a complete list of affected groups enough to issue one?

A complete list identifies the work that must be accounted for; it does not show that the work has reached durable aggregate state. Under this decision, a certificate must not attest to a group update that is merely staged. Completeness of coverage and completion of application are separate conditions.
What precisely must happen before issuance on the source side of a group move?

The required source-group removal must be durably applied before a certificate attests to it. If the transaction also changes the destination group, group-complete evidence must cover that required addition as well. The decision does not specify a particular acknowledgment format or how the system verifies durable application.
Does durable aggregate application mean the aggregate update has simply been queued for an asynchronous worker?

No. Queued or staged work is not yet durably applied work. The issuance condition concerns the aggregate state actually incorporating the required effect durably, rather than a promise to incorporate it later. The decision does not define the persistence mechanism or the operation that establishes durability.
If a source-group deletion was applied internally but is not durable yet, may its certificate be issued?

Not under the stated rule. Internal progress alone does not satisfy *durable aggregate application*. A failure before that effect becomes recoverable could leave the certificate attesting to an aggregate state that cannot be supported after recovery. That explains the ordering requirement without prescribing how durability is achieved.
Does this require every aggregate value in every group to change before a transaction can publish?

No. It concerns the updates the transaction actually requires in its affected groups. An unchanged displayed MIN or MAX does not necessarily mean a group had no required update: a counted value’s multiplicity might have changed. Conversely, unaffected groups do not need invented updates just to satisfy a group-complete certificate.
What is the separate role of atomic fence checkpoints?

They keep the recovered group-version fence consistent with the aggregate progress it is meant to protect. If the fence and group state recover from incompatible points, replay could be judged against a boundary that does not describe the recovered aggregate version. Requiring an atomic checkpoint alongside durable application addresses recovery-state consistency as a distinct prerequisite to certificate issuance.
Does an atomic fence checkpoint necessarily mean copying the entire aggregate index?

No such copying procedure is stated. “Atomic” describes the required consistency of the checkpointed fence with the relevant aggregate state, not its physical size or format. The decision does not specify checkpoint granularity, frequency, or storage layout.
Why put the fence checkpoint before issuing a group-complete certificate, rather than checkpoint it after publication?

The certificate is meant to support publication of aggregate state that recovery can continue to interpret correctly. If publication proceeds before the required fence state is atomically checkpointed, a later recovery could lack a reliable boundary for replay against that certified version. The decision therefore places atomic fence checkpoints before issuance, not as a repair to perform after the snapshot is exposed.
Does persisting a fence prove the aggregate value is mathematically right?

No. It preserves a version boundary consistently; it does not prove that SUM, COUNT, MIN, MAX, or a counted-tree update was calculated correctly. The certificate’s group coverage, durable application, atomic fence checkpoint, and agreement with full recomputation address different obligations.
How should the two prerequisites relate to each other if they are completed on different shards at different times?

Each affected group must have the required durably applied effect and an appropriate atomic fence checkpoint before group-complete evidence can attest to the transaction’s aggregate work. The shards need not finish their internal steps simultaneously. Publication must not treat the first completed side as proof that the other required side is ready.
Could one shard issue a group-complete certificate while the destination group on another shard remains staged?

Not a certificate that truthfully covers the complete transaction’s affected-group work. A staged destination update has not met the durable-application prerequisite. The decision does not prescribe whether evidence is packaged per shard, per group, or otherwise; whatever form it takes must not certify complete aggregate application prematurely.
Does the decision replace generation fencing with fence checkpoints?

No replacement is stated. A generation fence concerns whether publication evidence is applicable to the shard’s leadership context. An atomic group-version fence checkpoint concerns what version boundary recovery restores for the aggregate group. Retaining group-complete certificates while imposing durable application and atomic checkpoint prerequisites does not make those two kinds of fencing interchangeable.
What if a certificate has the right transaction digest and current shard generation?

Those properties do not waive the new issuance conditions. It must still not attest to an aggregate update before durable application, and the required fence checkpoint must be atomic. Correct identity and generation say which transaction and shard context the evidence concerns, not whether staged group work has reached a recoverable, consistently fenced state.
Can a checkpoint be atomic even if the source-group deletion has not been durably applied?

Checkpoint consistency alone does not establish completion of a required deletion. The decision requires *both* durable aggregate application and atomic fence checkpoints before certificate issuance. One prerequisite should not be treated as a substitute for the other.
Conversely, could the deletion be durable while the recovered fence still describes an earlier group version?

That is the sort of inconsistency the atomic fence-checkpoint condition is meant to exclude. Durable aggregate state and the fence recovered to govern replay need to describe compatible progress. The decision does not specify how the implementation makes that consistency atomic or handles an interrupted checkpoint.
What does the phrase “earlier passes missed both defects” authorize me to say?

You can state that earlier passes missed both defects: certification ahead of durable aggregate application and an inconsistent or stale fence checkpoint. The decision does not give a new numerical count for those passes or invite reconstructing their individual results. The point is that an earlier pass cannot be treated as sufficient evidence that either issuance prerequisite was already enforced.
Should I name particular earlier tests and their results to justify that sentence?

Not necessary. The current decision explicitly says earlier passes missed both defects. You can preserve that judgment without reconstructing test histories, assigning an earlier test a particular status, or adding measurements beyond this decision.
Is this decision itself evidence that both defects have now been removed?

No. It selects a stricter certificate-issuance rule in light of the stated limitation of earlier passes. It does not report an implementation of that rule, a new crash-recovery run, or a comparison showing that the resulting view matches recomputation.
If the issuance rule is enforced, may late replay overwrite a certified group version?

The checkpointed fence is intended to give recovery a consistent version boundary against which to judge replay. The decision does not specify a replay-write algorithm or establish that every possible late write is rejected correctly. It requires the fence to be atomically checkpointed before issuing evidence for durable aggregate work; protecting the published result still depends on that boundary being respected during recovery.
Does rejecting replay mean rejecting every update that arrives after certification?

No. A later legitimate transaction may need a newer aggregate version. The concern is an inapplicable write changing a version already certified for a committed snapshot. The decision does not prescribe a blanket rejection of later work or define how a particular replay record is classified.
How would this matter to per-group SUM/COUNT and counted MIN/MAX trees?

A required signed delta must be durably reflected in the affected group’s aggregate state before certification. That can change SUM or COUNT, a value’s multiplicity in a counted MIN/MAX tree, or a visible extremum. The checkpointed version fence must then remain consistent with that applied state across recovery. The decision does not specify aggregate expressions or a tree-update procedure.
Could a counted minimum stay unchanged even when the certificate must wait?

Yes. Retracting one of several equal minimum contributions can leave the displayed MIN unchanged while changing its count. If that removal is a required group update, it still must be durably applied, with an atomic fence checkpoint, before a group-complete certificate attests to it. Visible numerical change is not the test for application completeness.
Does issuing after durable application and checkpointing automatically make the source and destination aggregates equal recomputation?

No. It prevents certification of merely staged work and requires consistent recoverable fence state, but an applied delta could still have an incorrect value. Source and destination aggregates must independently agree with full recomputation for the same committed snapshot. The decision supplies no new comparison result.
Does this ordering require globally pausing writers?

No global pause is specified. Waiting to issue a certificate for the transaction’s affected groups is a condition on that transaction’s publication evidence, not an instruction to stop all writers. The decision gives no writer-progress measurement, so it also should not be presented as proof that unrelated writers never paused.
Does an atomic fence checkpoint require rescanning unaffected base-table partitions?

No such rescan is specified. Persisting group-version boundaries with aggregate checkpoint state is different from reading unrelated base-table partitions. Equally, the decision does not report an unaffected-partition scan count; avoiding those rescans remains a separate operational condition.
What must remain true if a crash occurs after aggregate application but before certificate issuance?

The work must not acquire a group-complete certificate merely because it was in progress before the crash. Recovery would need to establish that the required effects are durably present and that the appropriate fence state is atomically checkpointed before issuance. The decision defines those prerequisites but not the procedure for handling that particular crash boundary.
And if a crash occurs after a certificate is issued?

The certificate should be supported by durable aggregate application and an atomic fence checkpoint already in place. Recovery must still honor the version boundary when handling replay; the decision does not supply a failure trace or guarantee how a particular implementation behaves after the crash. Certificate issuance should not precede the recoverable state it attests.
How should I distinguish a certificate’s completeness from its truthfulness?

Completeness asks whether it covers all aggregate groups affected by the transaction. Truthfulness of the application claim asks whether those groups’ required effects were durably applied before issuance. Atomic fence checkpoints supply the recovery-consistency prerequisite. The decision retains completeness while explicitly adding the latter two requirements; checking only the list of groups would miss them.
Is there a compact publication invariant behind this decision?

Do not issue group-complete application evidence until every required affected-group update it attests is durably applied and the relevant group-version fences are atomically checkpointed; only then can that evidence be used toward publishing the transaction’s snapshot. This states the selected ordering without claiming that it has been verified in a subsequent run.
Give me one final sentence that keeps the explicit comparison with earlier passes but does not retell their history.
“Retain group-complete certificates, but issue them only after durable aggregate application and atomic fence checkpoints, because earlier passes missed both defects.”
